claim: The people who felt unsure were less interested in adding new traits, and less likely to pick up the partner's traits.
method: 152 participants were primed with low or high self-concept clarity, then reported interest in self-expansion and, in one study, rated themselves on attributes of a potential romantic partner.
post: Researchers made some people feel unsure about who they are, and others feel sure. Everyone then said how interested they were in adding new traits to themselves, and rated themselves on the traits of a possible romantic partner. The people who felt unsure were less interested in adding new traits, and less likely to pick up the partner's traits.

claim: People took longer and made more errors telling apart the mirror-image letters.
method: 48 participants completed a task in which they discriminated between pairs of letters that were lateral mirror images of each other (e.g., b/d) and pairs that were not (e.g., a/h), while reaction times and accuracy were recorded.
post: People judged whether two letters were the same or different. Some pairs of different letters were mirror images of each other, like b and d, and others were not, like a and h. People took longer and made more errors telling apart the mirror-image letters.

claim: The number of online friends predicted how much grey matter, the brain's working tissue, people had in three areas, including ones tied to social perception and memory.
journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
post: People's friend counts on a social networking site were recorded, and their brains were scanned. Some people had few online friends and others had many. The number of online friends predicted how much grey matter, the brain's working tissue, people had in three areas, including ones tied to social perception and memory.

claim: When people felt more favorable, they saw less risk and more benefit.
method: 219 participants read information designed to make their overall feelings about hazards such as nuclear power more or less favorable, then rated each hazard's risk and benefit.
post: People read information about hazards such as nuclear power. The information was written to make people feel more favorable or less favorable toward each hazard. Then they rated how risky and how beneficial it was. When people felt more favorable, they saw less risk and more benefit.

claim: Bilingual adults were worse than monolingual adults at noticing the second target when it came soon after the first.
method: 18 adults, monolingual and bilingual, completed a rapid serial visual presentation task measuring the attentional blink.
journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
post: People saw items flashed one after another very quickly and had to pick out two targets. Some of the adults spoke one language and some spoke two. Bilingual adults were worse than monolingual adults at noticing the second target when it came soon after the first.

claim: People who were told the result thought it was more likely to happen again.
method: 184 participants read descriptions of scientific studies and estimated the probability that the results would recur in future trials, either after being told the outcome or without being told it.
journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
post: People read about scientific studies and guessed how likely it was that the results would come out the same way again. Some were told how the study came out, and others were not. People who were told the result thought it was more likely to happen again.

claim: Students who thought intelligence can grow saw their grades climb, while students who thought it is fixed stayed flat.
method: 373 seventh graders reported whether they believed intelligence is malleable or fixed, and their mathematics grades were tracked over two years of junior high school.
post: Seventh graders said whether they thought intelligence can grow or is fixed. Then their math grades were followed for two years. Students who thought intelligence can grow saw their grades climb, while students who thought it is fixed stayed flat.

claim: Blood oxygen rose in two spots toward the back on each side, areas the researchers linked to the social brain network.
method: 36 five-month-old infants watched dynamic social videos of faces and hands, dynamic nonsocial motion, and static images while near-infrared spectroscopy measured blood oxygenation in their temporal lobes.
post: Babies were shown things to look at while a sensor measured blood oxygen in the sides of their brains, using light that passes through the scalp. Blood oxygen rose in two spots toward the back on each side, areas the researchers linked to the social brain network.

claim: People were more likely to say so when the action was bad.
method: 117 participants read scenarios in which an agent acted against their better judgment, with the action being either bad or neutral, and rated how much they agreed the agent showed weakness of will.
post: People read stories about someone who acted against their own better judgment. In some stories the action was bad and in others it was neutral. Then they rated how much the person showed weakness of will. People were more likely to say so when the action was bad.

claim: People who read what the person was doing rated the behavior as more intentional.
method: 48 participants read descriptions of a person's behavior phrased either as what the person was doing or as what the person did, then rated how intentional the behavior was.
post: People read descriptions of a person's behavior, written either as what the person was doing or as what the person did. Then they rated how intentional the behavior was. People who read what the person was doing rated the behavior as more intentional.

claim: Those prompted to think long were less likely to choose helping a colleague.
method: 555 employees were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: no instruction about time horizons, expanded time horizons, or limited time horizons. They then chose among helping a colleague, working on a career-advancing project, or working on a project taking the company in a new direction.
post: Employees chose between helping a colleague, a career-advancing project, or a project taking the company in a new direction. Some were first prompted to think of a long future at work, some a short one, and some not at all. Those prompted to think long were less likely to choose helping a colleague.

claim: Products with round logos were rated as more comfortable and less durable than products with angular logos.
method: 109 participants rated products on comfortableness and durability after seeing circular or angular logos.
post: People saw products with either a round logo or an angular one. Then they rated how comfortable and how durable each product seemed. Products with round logos were rated as more comfortable and less durable than products with angular logos.

claim: People were slower to call those wrong than wrong ones made from an already wrong sequence.
method: In two experiments (57 in the lab, 94 online), people made speeded grammaticality judgments about five-word sequences, including ungrammatical sequences formed by transposing two adjacent words from either a grammatical or an ungrammatical base sequence.
post: People quickly judged whether five-word sequences were grammatical. Some wrong ones were made by swapping two neighboring words in a correct sentence, like 'The white cat was big' becoming 'The white was cat big'. People were slower to call those wrong than wrong ones made from an already wrong sequence.

claim: More people agreed to receive it when they had to opt out.
method: 235 participants chose whether to receive health-related information under an opt-in default, an opt-out default, or no default.
post: People chose whether to receive health-related information. For some they had to opt in to get it, and for others they had to opt out to avoid it. More people agreed to receive it when they had to opt out.

claim: Women entered the competition more often under the rule that added to their score.
method: 72 people chose whether to compete in a calculation task under a control rule or under a rule that added one correct calculation to every woman's score.
post: People chose whether to enter a competition based on solving calculations. Under one rule nothing changed, and under another one extra correct calculation was added to every woman's score. Women entered the competition more often under the rule that added to their score.

claim: People thinking of big secrets overthrew more than people thinking of trivial secrets.
post: People were asked to think about either a big secret they were keeping or a trivial one. Then they did a throwing task, and researchers measured how far their throws went past the mark. People thinking of big secrets overthrew more than people thinking of trivial secrets.

claim: Thinking about regret stopped the worse third option from pushing people toward the more expensive choice.
method: Participants chose between two options in a personal preference task, with a decoy option added in some conditions; in one condition they were prompted to consider how much they might regret their choice.
post: People chose between two options. In some conditions a third, clearly worse option was added. Some people were also asked to think about how much they might regret their choice. Thinking about regret stopped the worse third option from pushing people toward the more expensive choice.

claim: People who had planned how to carry out their decision had less mixed feelings about those things.
method: Participants were assigned to plan the implementation of a decision, deliberate, or a control condition, then reported their attitudes toward various objects unrelated to the decision.
journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
post: Some people planned how they would carry out a decision. Others weighed up a decision, and others did neither. Then everyone said how they felt about several things unrelated to the decision. People who had planned how to carry out their decision had less mixed feelings about those things.

claim: People responded faster when the names matched.
method: 34 participants responded to visual target letters while hearing task-irrelevant auditory letters that were the same letter name, a different letter mapped to the same response, or an incongruent letter.
post: People responded to letters shown on a screen while hearing a letter spoken at the same time, which they were meant to ignore. Sometimes the spoken letter had the same name as the one on the screen, and sometimes it was a different letter. People responded faster when the names matched.

claim: People who read the literary fiction story did better than people who read the nonfiction article.
method: Adults read a short literary fiction story, a nonfiction article, a popular fiction story, or read nothing, then completed tests of affective and cognitive Theory of Mind.
post: Adults read a short literary fiction story or a nonfiction article. Then they took a test of how well they understand other people's emotions. People who read the literary fiction story did better than people who read the nonfiction article.

claim: People did worse when their smartphone was nearby than when it was in another room.
method: 275 people completed tasks measuring attention and memory with their smartphone either on the desk, in a pocket or bag, or in another room.
journal: Journal of the Association for Consumer Research
post: People did tasks that tested attention and memory with their own smartphone on the desk, in a pocket or bag, or in another room. People did worse when their smartphone was nearby than when it was in another room.

claim: Fair offers made people happier than unfair offers of the same value.
method: 12 adults received fair and unfair monetary offers matched for payoff while their brain activity was recorded and they rated their happiness.
post: Adults received money offers, some fair and some unfair, that were worth the same amount of money. They rated how happy each offer made them while their brain activity was recorded. Fair offers made people happier than unfair offers of the same value.

claim: People holding the heavy clipboard rated the candidates as more important.
method: 54 adults held a heavy or light clipboard while rating job candidates on a 1 to 7 scale of importance.
post: People held either a heavy clipboard or a light one while they rated job candidates on how important they seemed, from 1 to 7. People holding the heavy clipboard rated the candidates as more important.

claim: The more often they had given a particular answer before, the more likely they were to give it again, whether it was right or wrong.
method: 24 adults performed a serial recall task in which one sequence was repeated throughout the session while other sequences varied; the probability of each response was tracked across its prior occurrences.
journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
post: People tried to recall the same list of items in order, over and over, with new lists mixed in. The more often they had given a particular answer before, the more likely they were to give it again, whether it was right or wrong.

claim: People did better with the ball they believed was lucky.
method: 28 participants played a golf putting task with either a ball described as lucky or a neutral ball.
post: People played a golf putting game. Some were told the ball they were using was lucky, and others used a neutral ball. People did better with the ball they believed was lucky.

claim: People resisted going along with the statement more in the police story than in the myth.
method: 30 participants read stories in two genres, police procedural and Aztec myth, each containing the same morally deviant proposition, and rated their resistance to accepting it.
post: People read a story that contained a morally odd statement. Some read it as a police story and others as an Aztec myth, with the same statement in both. People resisted going along with the statement more in the police story than in the myth.

claim: Adults preferred to do it together anyway.
method: 20 adults chose between completing a task alone or together with a partner across five experiments where acting together cost more.
journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
post: Adults chose between completing a task alone or together with a partner. Doing it alone was the more effective way to reach the goal. Adults preferred to do it together anyway.

claim: When liberals and conservatives shared their views with no party labels showing, both got better at reading the data, and the gap between their beliefs disappeared.
method: 24 adults on Amazon's Mechanical Turk interpreted NASA climate communications in online networks, with partisanship made salient through party logos or political identity markers in some conditions.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
post: People read climate information from NASA online and shared what they thought it showed in small groups. Some groups had only liberals or only conservatives, and others had both. When liberals and conservatives shared their views with no party labels showing, both got better at reading the data, and the gap between their beliefs disappeared.

claim: The more of the things they wanted that people had, the happier they were.
method: 119 adults indicated whether they had and how much they wanted each of 52 material items; researchers computed how much each person had what they wanted and related it to happiness.
post: Adults said whether they owned each of 52 things and how much they wanted each one. Then they rated how happy they were. The more of the things they wanted that people had, the happier they were.

claim: When told to forget, people forgot the words they had seen twice more easily than those they had seen once.
method: 96 participants studied words presented once or twice, then were told to forget some of the words before recalling them.
journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
post: People studied words, some shown once and some shown twice. Then they were told to forget some of the words before recalling them. When told to forget, people forgot the words they had seen twice more easily than those they had seen once.

claim: People rated the decision as better when it turned out well.
method: 20 participants read matched descriptions of decisions that differed only in whether the outcome was a success or a failure, and rated the quality of each decision.
journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
post: People read descriptions of decisions that were identical except for how things turned out, a success or a failure. Then they rated how good each decision was. People rated the decision as better when it turned out well.

claim: People who recalled the unethical act felt less human than people who recalled the ethical act.
method: 156 participants recalled an unethical act, an ethical act, or a neutral event, then rated their human capabilities.
post: People recalled something unethical they did, something ethical they did, or a neutral event. Then they rated how human they felt. People who recalled the unethical act felt less human than people who recalled the ethical act.

claim: Four-year-olds picked the puppet that gave more chips, while five-year-olds started to look at what share of its chips each puppet gave.
method: Children played a Giving Game in which two puppets with different numbers of chips each gave some chips to the child, and children chose which puppet was nicer; adults did an analogous task.
post: Children played a game where two puppets, each starting with a different number of chips, gave some chips to the child. Then the child picked which puppet was nicer. Four-year-olds picked the puppet that gave more chips, while five-year-olds started to look at what share of its chips each puppet gave.

claim: Students who practiced recalling did better.
method: 40 students read science texts and either practiced retrieval or studied with concept mapping, then took a final test one week later.
post: Students read science texts. Some then practiced recalling what they had read, and others studied the texts by making concept maps. One week later everyone took a final test. Students who practiced recalling did better.

claim: Managers saw highly capable candidates as less committed and were less likely to offer them the job.
method: In four experiments, hiring managers evaluated candidates with varying levels of capability and decided whether to extend a job offer.
post: Hiring managers read about job candidates who were either highly capable or capable enough. They rated how committed each candidate would be to the organization and decided whether to offer a job. Managers saw highly capable candidates as less committed and were less likely to offer them the job.

claim: The people who expected to keep the mug asked for more money.
method: 112 subjects were randomly assigned a high or low probability of obtaining a mug, then reported the lowest price at which they would sell it.
post: Some people were told they would probably get a mug, and others that they probably would not. Then everyone named the lowest price they would sell the mug for. The people who expected to keep the mug asked for more money.

claim: Students who sought more reassurance scored lower on the ACT.
method: 151 college students completed a questionnaire measuring how often they seek reassurance about tests and gave access to their academic records, including ACT scores.
post: College students answered questions about how often they look for reassurance about tests. Researchers then looked up their ACT college entrance test scores in their academic records. Students who sought more reassurance scored lower on the ACT.

claim: People were more willing when he was described as less than human.
method: In vignette experiments, participants read a description of a stranger in dehumanizing or humanizing language and reported their willingness to harm him for money or for his immoral behavior.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
post: People read about a stranger, described either in words that made him seem less than human or in words that made him seem fully human. Then they said how willing they would be to break his thumb for money. People were more willing when he was described as less than human.

claim: People remembered more of the words they had rated for survival.
method: 24 participants rated words for survival relevance or for relevance to a contextually rich non-survival scenario, then recalled the words.
post: People rated words for how useful each would be in a survival situation, or in a richly described scenario that was not about survival. Then they recalled the words. People remembered more of the words they had rated for survival.

claim: Most took the sure thing when it was about lives saved, and the gamble when it was about deaths.
post: People chose between two programs where lives were at stake. One group read: 200 saved for sure, or a one-in-three chance of saving 600. Another read: 400 die for sure, or a one-in-three chance nobody dies. Most took the sure thing when it was about lives saved, and the gamble when it was about deaths.

claim: Middle-aged and older adults had more people who care about others than young adults did, and fewer of the other two types.
method: Adults completed measures of social value orientation and adult attachment style, and reported how many siblings they had.
journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
post: People were grouped by how they weigh other people's outcomes: caring about others, caring only about themselves, or wanting to beat others. Young, middle-aged, and older adults were compared. Middle-aged and older adults had more people who care about others than young adults did, and fewer of the other two types.

claim: People who got the word red scored lower than people who got the word gray.
method: 44 participants read the word 'red' or the word 'gray' before completing an achievement test.
post: Some people were subtly exposed to the word red, and others to the word gray. None of them guessed what the study was really about. Then everyone took a test. People who got the word red scored lower than people who got the word gray.

claim: Left-handed people judged both arms accurately.
method: 14 right- and left-handed participants looked at each arm and hand individually and judged their lengths.
post: Right-handed and left-handed people looked at each of their arms and hands one at a time and judged how long they were. Right-handed people judged their right arm and hand to be longer than their left. Left-handed people judged both arms accurately.

claim: People found the ads with the in-between steps more believable.
method: 213 consumers viewed ads for a desired change that showed either the starting and ending points alone or those points plus intermediate steps, then rated the ad's credibility.
post: People looked at ads that promised a change. Some ads showed just the before and after pictures, and others also showed pictures of the steps in between. People found the ads with the in-between steps more believable.

claim: People adjusted less away from the precise number than from the rounded one.
method: 59 participants made numerical estimates after seeing either a precise or a rounded anchor value.
post: People made a numerical estimate after seeing a starting number. For some the number was precise, and for others it was rounded. People adjusted less away from the precise number than from the rounded one.

claim: The people who wrote about God leaned more toward the computer.
method: Participants were prompted to think about God or not, then chose between a human and an AI recommendation in contexts such as entertainment, food, and dental procedures.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
post: Some people wrote about the role of God in their lives, and others wrote about their day. Then everyone chose whether to follow advice from a computer or from a human. The people who wrote about God leaned more toward the computer.

claim: Frequent users rated the characters as more pleasant after social media images than after the other images, while less frequent users rated them the same.
method: In two studies, 200 people who used social media frequently or infrequently saw social media and control images and rated the pleasantness of unrelated Chinese characters shown afterward.
post: People who use social media a lot and people who use it less saw social media images and other images. After each image they rated how pleasant an unrelated Chinese character looked. Frequent users rated the characters as more pleasant after social media images than after the other images, while less frequent users rated them the same.

claim: People did better on the task they thought they were unlikely to complete later than on the one they thought they were likely to complete.
method: 34 participants completed two tasks, one they were told they were likely to complete and one they were told they were unlikely to complete, and their performance on each was compared.
post: People worked on two different visual tasks. They believed they would probably do one of the tasks again later, and probably not the other. Which task was which varied across people. People did better on the task they thought they were unlikely to complete later than on the one they thought they were likely to complete.

claim: Both children and adults found the snake faster than the others.
method: In three experiments, 48 preschool children and adults searched an array of eight pictures for a single target picture, which was a snake or a nonthreatening flower, frog, or caterpillar.
post: Preschool children and adults looked at eight pictures at once and had to find one particular picture. Sometimes the picture they were looking for was a snake, and sometimes a flower, a frog or a caterpillar. Both children and adults found the snake faster than the others.

claim: People who thought about a recession felt their life had less meaning.
method: 121 participants were randomly assigned to think about a recession or about architecture, then rated how much meaning they felt in their life.
post: People were randomly asked to think about a recession or about architecture. Then they rated how much meaning they felt in their life. People who thought about a recession felt their life had less meaning.

claim: They were faster when the side words were 'farm' than when the side words were unrelated.
method: 30 participants made lexical decisions to central target words that were flanked on both sides by other words, which were either the target's stem, an embedded word, or an unrelated word.
post: People saw a word like 'farmer' in the middle of the screen with a word on each side. They had to decide whether the middle word was a real word. They were faster when the side words were 'farm' than when the side words were unrelated.

claim: Women reacted less negatively to the sexual imagery when the product was expensive than when it was cheap.
method: 87 adults viewed ads that paired a sexually charged or neutral scene with an expensive or cheap product, then rated their attitudes toward the imagery.
post: People looked at ads that put either a sexually charged scene or a neutral scene next to an expensive or a cheap product. Then they rated how they felt about the imagery. Women reacted less negatively to the sexual imagery when the product was expensive than when it was cheap.

claim: White and South Asian Londoners changed little.
method: A public attitudes survey was administered to Londoners at random times, and responses of 50 black Londoners before and after the killing of Eric Garner were compared with those of white and South Asian Londoners.
post: A public attitudes survey asked Londoners about their police, and the day each person was surveyed was random. Black Londoners surveyed after the police killing of Eric Garner in New York were less satisfied with London's police than those surveyed before. White and South Asian Londoners changed little.

claim: People could tell positive from negative by looking at the body alone, but not by looking at the face alone.
method: 15 viewers saw photographs of tennis players at peak emotional moments, showing either the isolated body, the isolated face, or the face together with the body, and rated the emotion.
post: People looked at photographs of tennis players at their peak emotional moments. Some saw only the body, some only the face, and some the face with the body. They rated how positive or negative the player felt. People could tell positive from negative by looking at the body alone, but not by looking at the face alone.

claim: In formal work messages, the sender who used smileys seemed less competent.
method: In three experiments, participants read work-related messages with or without a smiley and rated the sender's warmth and competence.
post: People imagined working on a team project and read a greeting from a teammate. Some greetings had smileys and some didn't. Then people rated the sender. In formal work messages, the sender who used smileys seemed less competent.

claim: The poorer people did worse on the test than the richer people.
method: 60 adults were primed with a financial problem suited to their income, then completed a cognitive control task measuring attention.
post: Poorer and richer people were asked to think about a money problem. Then they did a test of how well they could focus their attention. The poorer people did worse on the test than the richer people.

claim: After playing, people rated their ability higher.
method: 15,000 people played an online browser game in which they took the role of a fake news producer and learned six techniques used to make misinformation, rating their ability to spot and resist misinformation before and after.
post: People played an online game as a fake news producer and learned six tricks used to spread misinformation. Before and after playing, they rated their ability to spot and resist misinformation. After playing, people rated their ability higher.

claim: People who saw the cleaner streets were more satisfied than people who saw the dirtier ones.
method: 964 adults in an internet panel were randomly assigned to read low- or high-expectations statements from a hypothetical government official and to view low- or high-performance street cleanliness photographs.
journal: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management
post: People read a statement from a made-up government official that set low or high expectations for the city's services. Then they looked at photos of streets that were cleaner or dirtier and rated how satisfied they were with public services. People who saw the cleaner streets were more satisfied than people who saw the dirtier ones.

claim: The people who drank the bitter drink judged the misdeeds more harshly than the people who drank water.
method: 54 participants drank a sweet beverage, a bitter beverage, or water, then rated a variety of moral transgressions.
post: People drank a sweet drink, a bitter drink or water. Then everyone rated how wrong various moral misdeeds were. The people who drank the bitter drink judged the misdeeds more harshly than the people who drank water.

claim: People with a weak alternative made lower first offers than people with no alternative or a strong one.
method: 288 participants negotiated a simulated deal after being assigned a weak, no, or strong alternative; their first offers were recorded.
post: People negotiated a simulated deal after being given a weak alternative, a strong alternative, or no alternative. Researchers recorded each person's first offer. People with a weak alternative made lower first offers than people with no alternative or a strong one.

claim: People who thought they were unlikely to continue split the actions into fewer segments than people who thought they were likely to.
method: 21 participants watched a behavioral sequence after being told they were unlikely or likely to continue to the next part of the experiment and perform the observed actions, then segmented the sequence into units.
post: People watched a series of actions and split it into separate segments. Some believed they would probably go on to the next part of the experiment and do those actions themselves. Others believed they probably wouldn't. People who thought they were unlikely to continue split the actions into fewer segments than people who thought they were likely to.

claim: People judged on their decision process committed fewer resources to the failing project.
method: 60 participants made decisions about continuing to invest in a failing project under different accountability conditions, including being evaluated on their decision process versus a baseline.
post: People decided how much more to invest in a project that was failing. Some were told they would be judged on how they made the decision, and others had no such evaluation. People judged on their decision process committed fewer resources to the failing project.

claim: They still answered faster when the numbers were far apart in value than when they were close.
method: 32 Arabic speakers who used both Arabic and Indian numerals saw pairs of digits in the same or different notation and judged whether the digits were physically identical, ignoring their numerical values.
journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
post: Arabic speakers who use two sets of number symbols saw pairs of digits, written in the same set or in different sets. They only had to say whether the two digits looked identical, whatever their value. They still answered faster when the numbers were far apart in value than when they were close.

claim: People who read the neuroscience articles recommended shorter sentences and blamed the wrongdoer less.
method: 88 participants read neuroscience articles or other science articles, then recommended prison sentences and assigned blame for a transgressor.
post: People read either neuroscience articles about the brain basis of human behavior or other science articles. Then they recommended a prison sentence for a wrongdoer and said how much to blame the wrongdoer. People who read the neuroscience articles recommended shorter sentences and blamed the wrongdoer less.

claim: People who had thought about God were more willing to follow the AI's recommendation.
method: 349 participants were primed to think about God or not, then chose whether to follow an AI-recommended song.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
post: Some people were first led to think about God and others were not. Then everyone chose whether to follow a song recommended by artificial intelligence. People who had thought about God were more willing to follow the AI's recommendation.

claim: Shocks that came after a weak pulse were rated as less painful.
method: 20 adults received 25 painful electrical shocks to the arm, each either alone or preceded 40–60 ms earlier by a weak electrical pulse, and rated the pain of each shock.
post: Adults got 25 painful electric shocks to the arm and rated how much each one hurt. Some shocks came alone and some came a split second after a weak electrical pulse. Shocks that came after a weak pulse were rated as less painful.

claim: Relearning helped more for the pairs they had forgotten.
method: 240 participants studied category-exemplar pairs, practiced retrieving some pairs (causing forgetting of others), then relearned some forgotten and some non-forgotten pairs, and were finally tested on all pairs.
journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
post: People studied pairs of words, then practiced recalling some of them, which made them forget other related pairs. After that they studied some of the forgotten pairs again, along with some they hadn't forgotten. Relearning helped more for the pairs they had forgotten.

claim: When both were certain, people preferred the cash, but when each was only a tiny chance, they preferred the kiss.
method: 40 participants chose between a certain or low-probability kiss from a favorite movie star and a certain or low-probability $50 cash prize.
post: People chose between a kiss from their favorite movie star and $50 in cash. For some the choice was between getting each for sure, and for others between a tiny chance of each. When both were certain, people preferred the cash, but when each was only a tiny chance, they preferred the kiss.

claim: People in the US did the opposite.
method: 180 participants from Hong Kong and the United States estimated where high- and low-socioeconomic-status individuals live in a fictional city.
post: People in Hong Kong and in the US were asked where rich and poor people live in an imaginary city. Hong Kong people put the rich people in the south and the poor people in the north. People in the US did the opposite.

claim: Those told that scientists understand rated their own understanding higher.
method: 70 participants read about novel natural phenomena with no explanatory information and rated their own understanding; they were told either that scientists understood the phenomena or that scientists did not.
post: People read about unfamiliar natural events, with no explanation of how they work. Some were told that scientists understand the events, and others that scientists don't yet. Then everyone rated how well they understood the events themselves. Those told that scientists understand rated their own understanding higher.

claim: The distracted people spotted lies and truths more accurately than the others.
method: 66 participants watched videos of people lying or telling the truth, then either were distracted, were told to deliberate, or decided immediately, and judged which statements were lies.
journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
post: People watched videos of people lying or telling the truth, then judged which statements were lies. Some were distracted before deciding, some were told to deliberate, and some decided right away. The distracted people spotted lies and truths more accurately than the others.

claim: Students who wrote about their thoughts improved more from the first test to the second.
method: Students took a math pretest, then some wrote about their thoughts before a high-pressure posttest while others did not.
post: Students took a math pretest. Later they took a high-pressure math test, and some wrote about their thoughts right before it while others did not. Students who wrote about their thoughts improved more from the first test to the second.

claim: After the photos, people saw real motion as heading in the opposite direction.
method: 29 adults viewed a series of static photographs implying motion in one direction, then judged the direction of moving dot patterns.
post: People looked at a series of still photographs that implied movement in one direction. Then they judged which way patterns of moving dots were going. After the photos, people saw real motion as heading in the opposite direction.

claim: People thought a package held more food when it showed more product units.
method: 37 participants viewed packages of snack foods displaying different numbers of product units and judged how many items the package contained.
post: People looked at packages of snack foods that showed different numbers of product units on the front, and judged how many items each package contained. People thought a package held more food when it showed more product units.

claim: Negative news set off stronger bodily and emotional reactions than the other clips.
method: Participants in 17 countries watched real video news clips that were negative, neutral, or positive while their physiological reactions were recorded and they reported their feelings.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
post: People in 17 countries watched real news clips while their bodies were monitored and they reported their feelings. Some clips were negative, some neutral and some positive. Negative news set off stronger bodily and emotional reactions than the other clips.

claim: People whose life was going badly were more willing to stay connected.
method: 48 participants read a scenario in which their life was either negative or positive and chose whether to remain connected to an experience machine or return to reality.
post: People read about a virtual reality machine that provides pleasurable experiences. Some read that their life was going badly and others that it was going well. Then they chose whether to stay connected to the machine or return to reality. People whose life was going badly were more willing to stay connected.

claim: The Canadian-American athlete was seen as more Canadian when he won than when he lost.
method: 104 Canadian participants read about a fictional athlete with Canadian-American or Belgian-American dual nationality whose Olympic performance was described as a win or a loss, then rated his nationality.
post: Canadians read about a made-up Olympic athlete. He was either Canadian-American or Belgian-American, and he either won or lost. Then they rated how Canadian he was. The Canadian-American athlete was seen as more Canadian when he won than when he lost.

claim: People who read about rising inequality said being born wealthy matters more and hard work matters less.
method: 1,501 American adults read information about rising economic inequality in the United States or control information, then rated how important structural factors such as being born wealthy and individual factors such as hard work are for getting ahead.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
post: American adults read information about rising economic inequality in the United States, or read control information. Then they rated how important being born wealthy and how important hard work are for getting ahead. People who read about rising inequality said being born wealthy matters more and hard work matters less.

claim: They did not think they had eaten more, or feel any fuller.
method: 54 adults ate soup from bowls that either stayed at a normal level or slowly refilled unnoticed from below; researchers measured how much they ate and asked them to estimate their intake and fullness.
post: Some people ate soup from bowls that slowly and secretly refilled as they ate, and others ate from normal bowls. The people with the refilling bowls ate about 73% more soup. They did not think they had eaten more, or feel any fuller.

claim: Conservatives who read the purity version cared more about the environment.
method: In one study, 308 participants were presented with proenvironmental messages framed in terms of either purity or harm/care, and their environmental attitudes were measured.
post: People read messages urging them to protect the environment. Some messages talked about harm and care, and others about keeping nature pure and clean. Conservatives who read the purity version cared more about the environment.

claim: People were worse at telling the two flashes apart when a cue pointed to the spot.
method: 18 participants judged whether two successive flashes at the same location appeared as one or two, with the location either cued or not cued beforehand.
post: People watched two flashes of light appear one right after the other in the same spot and said whether they saw one flash or two. Sometimes a cue pointed to the spot just before, and sometimes not. People were worse at telling the two flashes apart when a cue pointed to the spot.

claim: Those who read about the demographic shift supported conservative positions more strongly.
method: White Americans read about the projected racial demographic shift toward a majority-minority nation or a control passage, then reported their support for conservative policy positions.
post: White Americans read about the projected shift toward a nation where racial minorities are the majority, or read a control passage. Then they reported how much they supported conservative policy positions. Those who read about the demographic shift supported conservative positions more strongly.

claim: The people with no control reported more than double the pain.
method: 100 participants were assigned to a lack-of-control or complete-control condition and then reported their physical pain.
post: Some people were put in a situation where they had no control over what happened, and others in one where they had complete control. Then everyone said how much physical pain they felt. The people with no control reported more than double the pain.

claim: People treated greedily passed on more greed than people treated generously passed on generosity.
method: In five experiments, 165 participants received a greedy, equal, or generous division of money or labor from an anonymous person, then divided additional resources with a different anonymous person.
post: People received a greedy, an equal or a generous split of money or work from an anonymous person. Then they divided more resources with a different anonymous person. People treated greedily passed on more greed than people treated generously passed on generosity.

claim: The signal that had never been unlearned set off a bigger sweat response and more of one kind of brain wave at the front of the head.
method: 42 healthy adults underwent fear conditioning, then extinction of one cue, and returned the next day for a recall test while scalp EEG and skin conductance were recorded.
post: People were taught to fear two signals, and then one of the two was unlearned. The next day both signals were shown again while their sweat and brain waves were recorded. The signal that had never been unlearned set off a bigger sweat response and more of one kind of brain wave at the front of the head.

claim: People did better on the questions when they were hard to read.
method: 41 participants answered reasoning questions printed in either a degraded, hard-to-read font or a normal, easy-to-read font.
post: People answered reasoning questions. For some, the questions were printed in a degraded, hard-to-read font, and for others in a normal, easy-to-read font. People did better on the questions when they were hard to read.

claim: The lesson lowered giving only for people who saw the girl.
method: 121 participants read about either an identifiable or statistical victim and were prompted to think deliberately or not, then decided how much money to donate.
journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
post: People finished a survey, were paid five one-dollar bills, and could donate any of it to Save the Children. Some read about one little girl with her picture, others read facts about hunger in Africa. Half also read a short lesson on how people give more to a single person than to statistics. The lesson lowered giving only for people who saw the girl.

claim: People said he did it on purpose more when the side effect was harmful than when it was helpful.
method: 77 people read a scenario in which a chairman's pursuit of profits also harmed or helped the environment, then rated whether he brought about the side effect intentionally.
post: People read about a chairman whose pursuit of profits also harmed or helped the environment. Then they rated whether he brought about that side effect on purpose. People said he did it on purpose more when the side effect was harmful than when it was helpful.

claim: People who did the puzzles first judged actions that harm some people to help others as more acceptable.
method: 92 subjects were randomly assigned to complete the Cognitive Reflection Test before or after responding to moral dilemmas, then rated the acceptability of utilitarian actions.
post: Some people solved a set of tricky puzzles before judging some moral dilemmas, and others solved them afterward. People who did the puzzles first judged actions that harm some people to help others as more acceptable.

claim: Their reading and their classroom behavior both improved from before the program to during it.
method: Six early elementary students were tracked on words read correctly per minute before and during an integrated academic and behavior intervention.
post: Six teachers ran a new extra-help program with second graders for 6 to 8 weeks. It worked on reading aloud smoothly and on staying engaged in class, together. Students were measured on both before and during the program. Their reading and their classroom behavior both improved from before the program to during it.

claim: The more open people were, the bigger the share they chose to read from senators of the other party.
method: 327 participants completed an 18-item self-report measure of receptiveness to opposing views and chose how much information to consume from U.S. senators representing their own party versus the opposing party.
post: People answered 18 questions about how open they are to opposing views. Then they chose how much to read from U.S. senators of their own party and from senators of the other party. The more open people were, the bigger the share they chose to read from senators of the other party.

claim: Simpler backgrounds led to more positive feelings on all four.
method: 30 participants viewed webpages with backgrounds of varying complexity and rated their attitudes toward the ad, brand, purchase intention, and website.
post: People looked at webpages with ads on backgrounds that were simple or complicated. Then they rated how they felt about the ad, the brand, buying the product and the website. Simpler backgrounds led to more positive feelings on all four.

claim: The White viewers said 'truth' more often for the Black speakers.
method: White participants watched videos of Black and White targets telling truths and lies about interpersonal relationships and judged whether each target was lying.
post: White people watched videos of Black and White speakers talking about their relationships. Some of the speakers told the truth and some lied, and the viewers judged which. The White viewers said 'truth' more often for the Black speakers.

claim: People with an Internet partner held the plank longer than people alone.
method: 115 adults played an exercise video game in a lab, holding abdominal planks as long as possible, then were randomly assigned to exercise alone, with an Internet partner, or with an encouraging Internet partner, and held planks again.
post: Adults played an exercise video game in which they held an abdominal plank as long as they could. Then some exercised alone and others with an Internet partner, and everyone held a plank again. People with an Internet partner held the plank longer than people alone.

claim: People in the high-power group rated it as more sarcastic than the low-power group did.
post: Some people were put in a frame of mind of having a lot of power, and others of having little. Then everyone rated how sarcastic a message would seem to a reader who lacked the sender's inside knowledge. People in the high-power group rated it as more sarcastic than the low-power group did.

claim: The people reminded of scarcity came up with more novel uses.
method: 133 participants were primed with resource scarcity or abundance in an unrelated context, then asked to generate novel uses for a given product.
post: Some people were reminded of scarcity and others of plenty. Then everyone had to come up with uses for a given product. The people reminded of scarcity came up with more novel uses.

claim: Prices moved farther away from the true worth when it went down.
method: 120 participants traded assets in experimental markets where the fundamental value either stayed constant or declined over time, and the ratio of cash to asset value either stayed constant or increased.
post: People traded assets in a market. In some markets what the asset was truly worth stayed the same over time, and in others it went down. Prices moved farther away from the true worth when it went down.

claim: African American professionals distrusted a workplace with few minorities that was colorblind rather than valuing diversity.
method: African American and White professionals read descriptions of workplace settings that varied in minority representation and diversity philosophy, then rated how much they trusted the setting.
journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
post: African American and White professionals read about workplaces that varied in how many minority employees they had and in whether they valued diversity or were colorblind. They rated how much they would trust each one. African American professionals distrusted a workplace with few minorities that was colorblind rather than valuing diversity.

claim: People who recalled the unethical deed were more likely to take the wipe.
method: 32 participants recalled either an unethical or an ethical deed and were then offered a choice between an antiseptic wipe and another product.
post: People recalled either an unethical deed or an ethical one. Then they were offered a choice between an antiseptic wipe and another product. People who recalled the unethical deed were more likely to take the wipe.

claim: After the demanding mental task, people gave up cycling sooner.
method: 16 adults cycled to exhaustion at 80% of peak power output after 90 minutes of a demanding cognitive task or 90 minutes of watching neutral documentaries.
post: Adults spent 90 minutes either doing a demanding mental task or watching emotionally neutral documentaries. Then they cycled at high intensity until they could not continue. After the demanding mental task, people gave up cycling sooner.

claim: People rated the products in vivid, highly saturated colors as larger.
method: Six experiments had participants view objects and products of various shapes and hues with high or low color saturation and rate their perceived size.
post: People looked at objects and products in colors that were either vivid or dull, and rated how big each one looked. People rated the products in vivid, highly saturated colors as larger.

claim: Those who thought about the friendly traits guessed the room was warmer than those who thought about the capable traits.
post: People thought about personality traits, either ones about being friendly and close to others or ones about being capable and getting things done. Then they estimated how warm the room was. Those who thought about the friendly traits guessed the room was warmer than those who thought about the capable traits.

claim: When the risk was changeable, big-picture thinking made people more eager to find out more.
method: 327 participants received negative feedback about a health risk described as changeable or unchangeable, and were prompted to think about it in broad, big-picture terms or in detailed, concrete terms, then rated their motivation to get supplementary information.
post: People were told something negative about a health risk, a risk described as either changeable or unchangeable. Some were asked to think about it in broad, big-picture terms, and others in concrete detail. When the risk was changeable, big-picture thinking made people more eager to find out more.

claim: Men were worse than women at telling the two apart.
method: 280 adults judged women's nonverbal cues as conveying friendliness or sexual interest, and their sensitivity to the distinction was compared between men and women.
post: Men and women judged whether women's nonverbal cues showed friendliness or sexual interest. Men were worse than women at telling the two apart.

claim: Right after seeing a new object, they were better at noticing a subtle change in a similar object than right after recognizing an old one.
method: 15 people viewed objects and judged whether each was new, familiar, or similar to one seen before; the accuracy of those judgments depended on whether the preceding object had been new or old.
post: People looked at a series of objects and said whether each was new, seen before, or similar to one seen before. Right after seeing a new object, they were better at noticing a subtle change in a similar object than right after recognizing an old one.

claim: The people who became unemployed changed more in agreeableness, conscientiousness and openness than the people who kept working.
method: 6,769 German adults rated their personality twice, four years apart; all were employed at the first rating, and some became unemployed or reemployed by the second.
post: Thousands of German adults who had jobs rated their personality, and then rated it again four years later. In between, some of them lost their jobs. The people who became unemployed changed more in agreeableness, conscientiousness and openness than the people who kept working.

claim: People primed to think analytically believed in conspiracy theories less.
method: 112 participants completed a scrambled-sentence task that primed analytic thinking or served as a control, then rated their belief in conspiracy theories.
post: People unscrambled sentences, some of which brought analytic thinking to mind and others not. Then they rated how much they believed in conspiracy theories. People primed to think analytically believed in conspiracy theories less.

claim: Donation rates were higher where people were donors unless they opted out.
method: Analysis of national organ donation rates across countries with opt-in, opt-out, and neutral donation systems, plus an experiment with 161 participants.
post: Countries were compared on how many of their people become organ donors. In some countries people are donors unless they opt out, and in others they are donors only if they opt in. Donation rates were higher where people were donors unless they opted out.

claim: The ones who feared seeming racist sat farther from the partner.
method: White participants anticipated a conversation with a Black partner under conditions designed to make the threat of appearing racist salient, and the physical distance they placed between themselves and the partner was measured.
journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
post: White people expected to have a conversation with a Black partner, about either racial profiling or love and relationships. Then the researchers measured how far apart they sat. The ones who feared seeming racist sat farther from the partner.

claim: The groups with money got more out of their trading.
method: 54 participants played a laboratory exchange game in groups with or without a money object, and their efficiency ratios were compared.
post: Groups played a trading game in a lab. Some groups had a money object to trade with and some did not. The groups with money got more out of their trading.

claim: People were less likely to say the person knew it when the stakes were high.
method: 264 participants read scenarios about a person in a high-stakes or low-stakes situation and rated whether the person knew, believed, guessed, or hoped something.
post: People read short stories about a person who thought something was true. In some stories the person would lose a lot if they were wrong, and in others very little. People were less likely to say the person knew it when the stakes were high.

claim: Poor people did about the same with or without a preview, while rich people did better with a preview than without.
method: 130 participants played a game in which they could borrow against future pay, with or without a preview of upcoming expenses.
post: People did a task in which some were in a poor group and others in a rich group. Within each group, some got a preview and some did not. Poor people did about the same with or without a preview, while rich people did better with a preview than without.

claim: People preferred thinking about it differently for the mild situations and distracting themselves for the intense ones.
method: 20 participants viewed emotional pictures or received unpredictable electric shocks that varied in intensity, then chose between reinterpreting the situation and distracting themselves.
post: People faced mild or intense upsetting pictures or electric shocks. Each time they chose between two ways to handle their feelings: thinking about the situation differently, or distracting themselves. People preferred thinking about it differently for the mild situations and distracting themselves for the intense ones.

claim: When the second ringed letter came soon after the first, people picked it out less often, more slowly and less precisely.
method: 12 adults watched streams of rapidly presented items and reported two targets; the timing between targets varied, and the errors people made were analyzed.
post: People watched letters flash by very fast, and two of the letters had a ring around them. They had to name both ringed letters. When the second ringed letter came soon after the first, people picked it out less often, more slowly and less precisely.

claim: People nudged to trust their gut contributed more than people nudged to reflect.
post: People played an economic game in which they chose how much of their own money to contribute, at a cost to themselves, to benefit others. Before playing, some were nudged to trust their gut feelings and others were nudged to think things over carefully. People nudged to trust their gut contributed more than people nudged to reflect.

claim: Attractiveness and earning prospects shaped romantic interest no differently for men than for women.
method: 163 speed daters rated their ideal partner preferences before an event, then rated romantic interest in partners met at the event and in write-ins afterward; researchers related those ratings to the partners' attractiveness and earning prospects.
journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
post: Before a speed-dating event, people rated what they wanted in an ideal partner. At the event they met partners and rated their romantic interest in each one. Researchers compared those ratings with each partner's attractiveness and earning prospects. Attractiveness and earning prospects shaped romantic interest no differently for men than for women.

claim: Asian American students were more motivated by their mothers than European American students were.
method: 117 high school students from Asian American and European American backgrounds experienced a failure and then reported their motivation from their mothers.
post: High school students, some Asian American and some European American, experienced a failure. Then they reported how motivated they felt by their mothers. Asian American students were more motivated by their mothers than European American students were.

claim: Men with antisocial personality disorder alone had committed more types of crimes than men with neither.
method: 390 incarcerated European American men were diagnosed with antisocial personality disorder, antisocial personality disorder plus psychopathy, or neither, and their criminal records were compared.
post: Researchers compared the criminal records of incarcerated men who had antisocial personality disorder, antisocial personality disorder plus psychopathy, or neither. Men with antisocial personality disorder alone had committed more types of crimes than men with neither.

claim: People searched more slowly while standing than while sitting.
method: 12 participants completed a visual search task with displays of four or eight items while seated and while standing; search rate per item was computed from response times.
post: People searched displays of four or eight items for a target, once while sitting and once while standing. People searched more slowly while standing than while sitting.

claim: The same parent was the more popular answer to both questions.
method: 170 people read a custody case and chose which parent should be awarded the child and which should be denied the child.
post: People read a custody case about two parents. Some were asked which parent should be awarded the child, and others which should be denied the child. The same parent was the more popular answer to both questions.

claim: People who saw three 6's guessed a longer sequence than people who saw two 6's or the mix.
method: 80 participants estimated the length of a sequence of die rolls after seeing either three 6's, two 6's, or a random sequence of two 6's and a 3.
post: People saw some die rolls: three 6's, two 6's, or two 6's and a 3. Each person guessed how long the whole sequence of rolls had been. People who saw three 6's guessed a longer sequence than people who saw two 6's or the mix.

claim: People rated harm from doing nothing as less immoral than harm from doing something.
method: 57 participants read scenarios pairing an omission with a commission while intentions, motives, and consequences were held constant, then rated the morality of the actor's choice or the goodness of the decision option.
post: People read stories in which a harmful outcome could come from doing something or from doing nothing, with the person's intentions, motives and the outcome the same. They rated how immoral the person's choice was. People rated harm from doing nothing as less immoral than harm from doing something.

claim: When the hidden picture was erotic, people picked the right curtain more often than chance.
method: 100 participants guessed the future location of erotic pictures on a computer screen before the pictures were randomly selected and displayed.
journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
post: People saw two curtains on a screen and guessed which one hid a picture. Only after they guessed did the computer randomly pick which side the picture was on. When the hidden picture was erotic, people picked the right curtain more often than chance.

claim: Men outperformed women when the test was framed as spatial but not when it was framed as social.
method: 139 participants completed perspective-taking tests framed as measuring either spatial ability or social (empathetic) ability, with the social version including human figures.
post: People took a perspective-taking test. Some were told it measured spatial ability, and others that it measured empathy, with human figures added to the empathy version. Men outperformed women when the test was framed as spatial but not when it was framed as social.

claim: People remembered a circle as larger when it was among larger circles of the same color, and smaller when it was among smaller ones.
method: 21 adults briefly viewed displays of colored circles of varying sizes, then reported the size of one tested circle.
post: People briefly viewed a display of colored circles of different sizes, then reported the size of one circle they were asked about. People remembered a circle as larger when it was among larger circles of the same color, and smaller when it was among smaller ones.

claim: The people who drank sugar valued the larger, later amount more than the people who drank artificial sweetener.
method: 65 participants drank a soft drink containing either sugar or artificial sweetener, then chose repeatedly between a smaller immediate amount of money and a larger amount later.
post: People drank a soft drink that had either sugar or artificial sweetener. Then they chose again and again between a smaller amount of money now and a larger amount later. The people who drank sugar valued the larger, later amount more than the people who drank artificial sweetener.

claim: The treated children had higher IQ and adaptive behavior scores than the children in special education.
method: 42 children with autism were assigned by parental preference either to 35 to 40 hours per week of early intensive behavioral treatment from a community agency or to special education classes, and were assessed on IQ, language, nonverbal skill, and adaptive behavior over three years.
post: Children with autism either got 35 to 40 hours a week of early intensive behavioral treatment from a community agency or went to special education classes, as their parents chose. Researchers tested their IQ and adaptive behavior over three years. The treated children had higher IQ and adaptive behavior scores than the children in special education.

claim: The people nudged to compare were more willing to wait.
method: 207 participants were randomly assigned to conditions promoting either comparative search, comparing features across options, or integrative search, combining features within an option, then made intertemporal choices.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
post: People chose between less money soon and more money later. Some were nudged to line the two offers up and compare them side by side. Others were nudged to look at one offer at a time. The people nudged to compare were more willing to wait.

claim: People who like thinking hard enjoyed it less after being told it was good, while people who don't enjoyed it more.
method: 160 people varying in need for cognition watched a relatively unfunny film clip after being given a positive expectation or no expectation, then rated their affective reactions.
post: People watched a film clip that wasn't very funny. Some were told beforehand that it was good, and others were told nothing. People who like thinking hard enjoyed it less after being told it was good, while people who don't enjoyed it more.

claim: After the hard questions, computer-related words came to mind more readily than other words.
method: 46 participants answered a series of difficult trivia questions, then named the ink color of computer-related and general words as quickly as possible.
post: People answered a series of difficult trivia questions. Then they named the ink color of words as fast as they could, some about computers and some not. After the hard questions, computer-related words came to mind more readily than other words.

claim: Older adults donated less to people they were not related to than younger adults did, but gave more time to relatives.
method: 89 younger and 66 older adults completed a hypothetical donation task, choosing how much money and time to donate to relatives and nonrelatives at varying social distances.
journal: The Journals of Gerontology: Series B
post: Younger and older adults imagined donating money and time to relatives and to people they were not related to, at different levels of closeness. Older adults donated less to people they were not related to than younger adults did, but gave more time to relatives.

claim: Those who had recalled being disrespected were more cynical.
method: 223 participants were assigned to recall an experience of being disrespected or a control experience, then reported their cynical beliefs about people.
post: Some people were asked to recall a time they were treated with disrespect, and others to recall an ordinary experience. Then everyone rated how selfish and untrustworthy they think people are. Those who had recalled being disrespected were more cynical.

claim: The lonely people believed more in supernatural beings and saw more social traits in their pets.
method: 57 participants were induced to feel lonely, fear, or a control state, then rated their belief in supernatural agents and the social traits of pets.
post: Some people were made to feel lonely, some scared and some neither. Then everyone rated how much they believed in supernatural beings, and how many social traits their pets had. The lonely people believed more in supernatural beings and saw more social traits in their pets.

claim: Afterwards, the ones who tried to change their feelings said it took more effort than just watching.
method: 58 participants watched an upsetting movie after being told either to watch it, to decrease their emotional response, or to increase their emotional response, then rated how much effort the instructions took.
journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
post: People watched an upsetting movie. Some were told just to watch it, some to feel less, and some to feel more. Afterwards, the ones who tried to change their feelings said it took more effort than just watching.

claim: Those who read the masculine-only form named fewer women than the others.
method: 90 native German speakers named their favorite musicians after reading words in one of three forms: masculine generics, feminine-masculine word pairs, or capital I forms.
journal: Journal of Language and Social Psychology
post: German speakers read words for groups of people, either in the usual masculine form or in forms that also name or include women. Then they named their favorite musicians. Those who read the masculine-only form named fewer women than the others.

claim: They guessed too few were good and too many were bad, and the more comments a supplier had, the bigger the mistake.
method: 39 participants acted as managers choosing among three providers in two product domains based on positive and negative feedback from a computerized database, then inferred actual differences.
journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
post: People took the role of a buyer choosing between three suppliers. They read a few customer comments about each one, then guessed how many of all its comments were good and how many were bad. They guessed too few were good and too many were bad, and the more comments a supplier had, the bigger the mistake.

claim: People who thought about a recession gave more to girls than people who thought about an upswing.
method: 198 adults were primed with economic recession or upswing conditions and then decided how to allocate resources between girls and boys.
post: People were led to think about an economic recession or an economic upswing. Then they decided how to split resources between girls and boys. People who thought about a recession gave more to girls than people who thought about an upswing.

claim: People who had thought about God were more willing to consider AI advice than people who had not.
method: Eight preregistered experiments with 2,462 participants made God salient and measured willingness to consider AI-based recommendations across contexts such as entertainment, food, mutual funds, and dental procedures.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
post: Some people were made to think about God, and others were not. Everyone then said how willing they were to consider advice from artificial intelligence. People who had thought about God were more willing to consider AI advice than people who had not.

claim: The average of the two guesses was closer to the truth than the first guess alone.
method: 173 people made two guesses about an unknown quantity, with a delay between the guesses, and the error of the average of the two guesses was compared with the error of the first guess.
post: People guessed something they did not know, then guessed again after a delay. Researchers averaged each person's two guesses. The average of the two guesses was closer to the truth than the first guess alone.

claim: People's hand movements wavered more on the partly true, partly false statements.
method: 141 participants moved a handle to one of two response options to agree or disagree with statements that varied in how true they seemed, and the path of each movement was recorded.
post: People agreed or disagreed with statements by moving a handle toward one of two answers, while the path of the movement was recorded. Some statements seemed clearly true, some clearly false, and some partly true and partly false. People's hand movements wavered more on the partly true, partly false statements.

claim: The listeners rated the Tagalog speakers as less competent and harder to understand.
method: 96 English-speaking listeners from Calgary rated audio recordings of 12 speakers (6 first-language English, 6 first-language Tagalog) on competence, treatment preference, and comprehensibility in work-related scenarios.
post: People in Calgary listened to recordings of workers speaking English. Some of the speakers were native English speakers and some were native Tagalog speakers. The listeners rated the Tagalog speakers as less competent and harder to understand.

claim: At this distance, that speed advantage did not show up.
method: Participants performed a spatial compatibility task in which a stimulus appeared on one side and they responded on a matching or non-matching side, while a partner sat far away.
post: Two people sat in the same room, each doing half of a reaction-time task by responding to just one of two possible signals. They sat farther apart than arm's reach. Sitting close, people usually respond faster when a signal appears on the same side as their response. At this distance, that speed advantage did not show up.

claim: The giver of the cheaper scarf was rated more generous than the giver of the coat.
method: 83 people read about a gift giver and rated how generous that person was; some saw a $45 scarf and others a $55 coat, each evaluated on its own.
post: People read about someone giving a gift, either a $45 scarf or a $55 coat. Each person read about only one of them and rated how generous the giver was. The giver of the cheaper scarf was rated more generous than the giver of the coat.

claim: People who had first refused the extreme favor were more likely to agree to the small one.
method: In three experiments, 72 participants were asked for a small favor either alone or after first refusing an extreme favor.
journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
post: Some people were asked for a small favor. Others were first asked for an extreme favor, which they refused, and then asked for the small favor. People who had first refused the extreme favor were more likely to agree to the small one.

claim: They reported stronger emotion while looking ahead to it than while remembering it.
method: 49 women rated their mood while anticipating their next menstrual period and while remembering their last one.
post: Women rated their mood while thinking about their next menstrual period, and again while remembering their last one. They reported stronger emotion while looking ahead to it than while remembering it.

claim: The tighter the resource, the more people gave up less important goals instead of stretching it.
method: 102 participants made plans for managing a limited resource under varying levels of constraint; their plans were coded as efficiency or priority strategies.
post: People made plans for managing a limited resource when it was more or less tight. Some plans stretched the resource to make it last, and others gave up less important goals to save it. The tighter the resource, the more people gave up less important goals instead of stretching it.

claim: People judged the concrete wording as more likely to be true.
method: 46 participants read statements of identical content, each written in either concrete or abstract language, and rated how probably true each statement was.
