post: Students in an online graduate course switched back and forth, week by week, between two ways of learning. In some weeks they did an activity called interteaching, and in the others they used an online discussion forum. Quiz scores were higher in the interteaching weeks than in the discussion forum weeks.

claim: Five of the six children began using the passive form after hearing it, compared with before.
post: Preschoolers took turns with an adult describing drawings of animals, like an elephant pulling a mouse. The adult always used the passive form ("The mouse is being pulled by the elephant") and gave stickers only for the plain active form. Five of the six children began using the passive form after hearing it, compared with before.

claim: Scores on the two versions lined up almost perfectly, a .999 match where 1.0 is perfect.
post: People's scores on an adult IQ test were compared across two versions. One was the standard test. The other was a shortened one that skips the easy early questions on some sections, based on how well a person did on the general-knowledge section. Scores on the two versions lined up almost perfectly, a .999 match where 1.0 is perfect.

claim: In both groups, the body's signals seemed to react to a future event the person couldn't know about, beyond what chance would produce.
post: People did a computer task while sensors tracked their sweat and heartbeat. Some were repeat entrepreneurs in the UK, others were non-entrepreneurs in the US. In both groups, the body's signals seemed to react to a future event the person couldn't know about, beyond what chance would produce.
journal: International Journal of Entrepreneurship and Small Business

claim: Husbands were somewhat more satisfied with their marriages than wives were.
post: Married people filled out a long questionnaire about their marriage. It covered things like sex, communication, parenting, and religion. The answers from husbands were compared with the answers from wives. Husbands were somewhat more satisfied with their marriages than wives were.

claim: The link between childhood trauma and these mild symptoms differed depending on which version of the gene a woman carried.
post: Women who are twins filled out a questionnaire about hard experiences in childhood and another about mild signs of psychosis. They also gave DNA samples. Researchers compared people carrying different versions of a gene linked to how the body handles stress. The link between childhood trauma and these mild symptoms differed depending on which version of the gene a woman carried.

claim: Their feelings were mixed: good about personal growth and schoolwork, bad about relationships with other people.
post: Gifted teenagers answered open-ended questions about what being gifted means to them and how they think other people see it. They felt positive about their own giftedness but did not think others did. Their feelings were mixed: good about personal growth and schoolwork, bad about relationships with other people.

claim: Allowing for how religious they were, hijab wearers had a more positive body image and cared less about appearance than women who never wore one.
post: Muslim women in Britain filled out questionnaires about their bodies, beauty in the media, and how religious they were. Some never wore a hijab (a head covering); others wore one at least rarely. Allowing for how religious they were, hijab wearers had a more positive body image and cared less about appearance than women who never wore one.

claim: Children with higher scores on the emotion test coordinated their actions better with their partner, even when age, gender and solo skill on the task were accounted for.
post: Children did a hands-on problem-solving task twice, once alone and once with another child. They also took a test of how well they understand emotions. Children with higher scores on the emotion test coordinated their actions better with their partner, even when age, gender and solo skill on the task were accounted for.

claim: The word-face matches could be explained by two underlying dimensions, and the same structure held for every age group.
post: Children and adults were given words like happy, scared, angry and sleepy, and matched each word to photos of actors making different faces. The children were 3, 4 or 5 years old. The word-face matches could be explained by two underlying dimensions, and the same structure held for every age group.

claim: The score predicted who would commit a violent offense after release in each of five subgroups of the men.
post: Men who had been charged with serious crimes were tracked after release. About half had been treated in a maximum security psychiatric hospital, and the rest were briefly assessed before prison. Researchers combined 12 pieces of information about each man into one score. The score predicted who would commit a violent offense after release in each of five subgroups of the men.

claim: Compared with before, patients were rated as less outgoing, less organized and dependable, less open to new things, and more prone to distress.
post: Caregivers of people with memory problems filled out a personality questionnaire about the patient twice: once for who the patient is now, and once for who they were before the memory problems. Compared with before, patients were rated as less outgoing, less organized and dependable, less open to new things, and more prone to distress.

claim: People who scored low on assertiveness reported fewer helpful thoughts and more unhelpful thoughts than people who scored high.
post: College students faced made-up situations with unreasonable requests, like three people they knew only slightly asking to cut in front of them in a movie line, and responded. Afterward they rated how often they had thoughts that made refusing easier or harder. People who scored low on assertiveness reported fewer helpful thoughts and more unhelpful thoughts than people who scored high.
journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology

claim: Of four considerations, how much they felt the crime needed punishment was most clearly linked to their choice.
post: Legal professionals watched a video summing up a court case in which a man badly hurt his former boss. The man's diagnosis varied: schizophrenia, a personality disorder, or an unnamed condition. Viewers chose a sentence. Of four considerations, how much they felt the crime needed punishment was most clearly linked to their choice.
journal: International Journal of Law and Psychiatry

claim: People who watched a partner stay switched less than both other groups; those who watched one move on switched more than the comparison.
post: Adults watched their romantic partner work on unsolvable puzzles, then tried them too. Partners were told to stay on one puzzle or to move to the next; a third group was the comparison. People who watched a partner stay switched less than both other groups; those who watched one move on switched more than the comparison.

claim: Agents were right 42% of the time with one set and 78% with another.
post: U.S. Customs agents watched videos of people being questioned and judged whether each person was lying. The people in the videos had been asked one of three different sets of questions, and the sets differed in how useful they were for exposing lies. Agents were right 42% of the time with one set and 78% with another.

claim: When people had been acting more outgoing or organized, they felt happier and less tired right then, but more tired about three hours later.
post: For 12 days, people got a prompt on their phones five times a day. Each time they rated how outgoing and how organized they had been acting, plus their mood and tiredness. When people had been acting more outgoing or organized, they felt happier and less tired right then, but more tired about three hours later.

claim: When sound and lips didn't match, adults reported hearing "da," but they heard the sound correctly without the video.
post: People watched a film of a young woman's face saying a syllable over and over. The sound was "ba," but her lips were moving for "ga." Others heard the same sound with no video, or watched an untouched film. When sound and lips didn't match, adults reported hearing "da," but they heard the sound correctly without the video.

claim: People with different versions of two dopamine-related genes scored differently on the social measures.
post: People answered questionnaires on mobile devices about their close friends, family, and romantic relationships. They also gave a saliva sample so researchers could check small differences in their genes. People with different versions of two dopamine-related genes scored differently on the social measures.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

claim: Question learners were slowed on those words right after learning and the next day; study-only learners were not slowed right after.
post: People learned made-up names for 16 unusual animals, either by studying each animal and its name or by answering a question about each animal. Later, everyone was tested on real words that look like a new name, like "tomato" for "torato." Question learners were slowed on those words right after learning and the next day; study-only learners were not slowed right after.

claim: The answers split into two groups: one about good effects of cannabis on sleep, the other about bad effects.
post: College students filled out an online survey of 12 statements about what they expect cannabis to do to their sleep. The researchers looked at which statements people tended to answer alike. The answers split into two groups: one about good effects of cannabis on sleep, the other about bad effects.

claim: Oxytocin greatly increased felt empathy, but not accuracy at guessing feelings, compared with placebo.
post: Men got a nasal spray with either oxytocin, a bonding hormone, or no active ingredient. Then they viewed pictures of people in happy or upsetting scenes, rating how much they felt for each person and guessing their feelings. Oxytocin greatly increased felt empathy, but not accuracy at guessing feelings, compared with placebo.

claim: Japanese children placed the horizon higher on the page than Canadian children did, and they included more pieces of information.
post: Schoolchildren in Canada and Japan, from first through sixth grade, were asked to draw a landscape. A second group made landscape collages from ready-made items. Japanese children placed the horizon higher on the page than Canadian children did, and they included more pieces of information.

claim: The separate test found the taught reason in all six children and added no false extra reason.
post: Six children were taught to touch a foam cushion to get an item, attention, or a break from tasks. Then each child got two tests of why a child acts out: one checks each reason separately, the other mixes them together. The separate test found the taught reason in all six children and added no false extra reason.

claim: Responses were faster when the word's meaning matched the word they had to say than when it didn't.
post: People saw words on a screen and had to say "positive" or "negative" out loud, depending on whether the word was a noun or an adjective. They were told to ignore what the word meant. Responses were faster when the word's meaning matched the word they had to say than when it didn't.

claim: Students told their rank were more likely to request it than the others.
post: Heavy-drinking students got four weekly messages about alcohol. Some got the official guidelines or how they compared with them, some how they compared with the average, and some how they ranked among others. Then they could request health information. Students told their rank were more likely to request it than the others.

claim: Afterward, 64% still had one, and three months later 50% did.
post: People with PTSD and a severe mental illness, such as schizophrenia or bipolar disorder, took part in a 12- to 16-week talk therapy program. It taught them about trauma, had them practice calming breathing, and helped them rethink troubling thoughts. Everyone started out with a PTSD diagnosis. Afterward, 64% still had one, and three months later 50% did.

claim: People rated the headlines they had seen before as less unethical to share, even when the headlines were clearly labeled as false.
post: People saw some fake-news headlines one time or four times, and other headlines not at all. Later they rated how unethical it would be to publish and share each headline. People rated the headlines they had seen before as less unethical to share, even when the headlines were clearly labeled as false.

claim: People in the control group cut back on the action that earned the food they were full of, but the stressed people did not.
post: People learned two actions that each earned a different food reward. Then they ate one of the foods until they were full of it. Before choosing again, some had a stressful cold-water test while being watched, and others had a control task. People in the control group cut back on the action that earned the food they were full of, but the stressed people did not.

claim: The best-fitting arrangement had three layers: one broad factor of general distress, two middle groups (anxious-misery and fears), and five narrow groups of more specific symptoms.
post: High school juniors were assessed for symptoms of anxiety and depression, and the researchers tested how those symptoms group together. The best-fitting arrangement had three layers: one broad factor of general distress, two middle groups (anxious-misery and fears), and five narrow groups of more specific symptoms.

claim: Only with eye movements did the re-recalled picture become less vivid, on the ratings and on the reaction-time task.
post: Students looked at two pictures, recalled them, and rated how vivid each memory felt. Then one picture was recalled again, with eye movements for one group and without them for the other. Afterward, they judged whether picture fragments were ones they had seen. Only with eye movements did the re-recalled picture become less vivid, on the ratings and on the reaction-time task.

claim: After the same or a similar picture, people pressed the key tied to the original faster than other keys.
post: People pressed one of four keys when a box lit up, and each key always showed a picture, like a banana. Later the picture came first: the same one, a similar new one like a pineapple, or a body part. After the same or a similar picture, people pressed the key tied to the original faster than other keys.

claim: After communication, scores on knowing your partner and on life skills predicted good relationships best, compared with the other skills.
post: People took an online quiz that scored seven relationship skills, including communication, stress management and knowing their partner. They also reported how well their romantic relationships were going. After communication, scores on knowing your partner and on life skills predicted good relationships best, compared with the other skills.

claim: Their behaviors changed over the course of the therapy, both in statistical tests and in a descriptive look at them.
post: One person with long-standing dramatic, attention-seeking and self-centered behaviors went through a fairly short course of talk therapy about how they relate to other people. There was no comparison group, only the same person tracked across sessions. Their behaviors changed over the course of the therapy, both in statistical tests and in a descriptive look at them.

claim: The symptoms fell into three clusters in the first group, and the same three clusters appeared in the second.
post: People with depression filled out a checklist of symptoms before starting treatment. Researchers looked at which symptoms tended to go together in one large group of patients, then checked a second, separate group. The symptoms fell into three clusters in the first group, and the same three clusters appeared in the second.

claim: With each older age group, people recalled relatively fewer negative pictures compared with positive and neutral ones.
post: Younger, middle-aged, and older adults looked at pictures on a computer screen. After a distraction task, they tried to recall as many pictures as they could. Some pictures were positive, some negative, and some neutral. With each older age group, people recalled relatively fewer negative pictures compared with positive and neutral ones.

claim: Medication was rated the least acceptable of all the options.
post: Teachers listened to a recording about a child who was either withdrawn or aggressive. Then they heard a second recording describing several ways to help, including family therapy, time out, play therapy and medication. They rated how acceptable each one seemed. Medication was rated the least acceptable of all the options.

claim: Apart from how classmates saw them, the kids with the illness did not differ from their classmates on those emotional measures.
post: Kids with sickle cell disease, a long-term blood illness, were compared with classmates from the same classrooms. Classmates described how sociable, accepted and aggressive each child seemed, and the kids were also measured on many signs of emotional well-being. Apart from how classmates saw them, the kids with the illness did not differ from their classmates on those emotional measures.

claim: Students who had the session took part more in class, showed more positive academic behavior, and got higher fourth-quarter math grades than the waiting group.
post: Middle school students were randomly put into two groups. One group had a single counseling session meant to help them find their own reasons to change, and the other group waited. Students who had the session took part more in class, showed more positive academic behavior, and got higher fourth-quarter math grades than the waiting group.

claim: Students who scored higher on the puzzles tended to score higher on the three main IQ scores.
post: College students solved puzzles about made-up three-letter words, deciding whether two words meant the same or the opposite, or whether one meant more or less. They also took a full standard IQ test. Students who scored higher on the puzzles tended to score higher on the three main IQ scores.

claim: Students taught the new method scored higher on the words they had been taught.
post: Sixth graders with learning disabilities, many still learning English, were in special education reading classes. Teachers in some schools spent about 15 minutes a day teaching four new school words a week. Another school did not get the new method. Students taught the new method scored higher on the words they had been taught.

claim: Flashing cleaner or corner affected responses to the next word about equally, and differently from brothel.
post: People decided as fast as they could whether letter strings on a screen were real words. Just before each one, another word flashed too briefly to notice: cleaner before CLEAN, corner before CORN, or brothel before BROTH. Flashing cleaner or corner affected responses to the next word about equally, and differently from brothel.

claim: Sad children were rated most believable, and children showing positive emotion least.
post: People watched videos of child actors telling police a made-up story of being physically abused. The child showed different emotions in different videos. Viewers rated how believable the child was and how likely the accused person was guilty. Sad children were rated most believable, and children showing positive emotion least.

claim: The one rated hardest of all was making a mistake that seriously injured or killed a fellow officer.
post: Police officers read a list of 34 things that can happen on the job. They rated how hard each one would be for officers to cope with, from 0 to 4. The one rated hardest of all was making a mistake that seriously injured or killed a fellow officer.

claim: The students who got the hard test scored higher on test anxiety than the students who got the easy test.
post: Junior high students were randomly given either a hard vocabulary test they would likely fail or an easy one they would likely pass. Right afterward, all of them filled out a questionnaire measuring test anxiety. The students who got the hard test scored higher on test anxiety than the students who got the easy test.

claim: For women who had already chosen to have the breast removed, the students recommended rebuilding the breast for 95% of the younger women but only 65% of the older women.
post: Second-year medical students read about eight women with similar-stage breast cancer and said what treatment they would recommend for each. Some of the women were 31 or younger and others were 59 or older. For women who had already chosen to have the breast removed, the students recommended rebuilding the breast for 95% of the younger women but only 65% of the older women.

claim: How strongly stress went with burnout depended on how resilient the women were.
post: Women social workers in a South Indian city filled out questionnaires about how stressed they felt, how well they bounce back from hardship, and how burned out they felt at work. Women with higher and lower resilience scores were compared. How strongly stress went with burnout depended on how resilient the women were.

claim: People with OCD were worse at forgetting the negative words than the positive and neutral ones, while people without OCD showed no such gap.
post: People with OCD and people without it saw a series of negative, positive, and neutral words. After each word, they were told to either remember it or forget it. Then everyone was tested on all the words. People with OCD were worse at forgetting the negative words than the positive and neutral ones, while people without OCD showed no such gap.

claim: Conversations with a phone present came out worse on closeness, connection, and conversation quality than conversations without one.
post: Two people sat down to have a face-to-face conversation. In some pairs a mobile phone was present, and in others there was no phone. Conversations with a phone present came out worse on closeness, connection, and conversation quality than conversations without one.
journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships

claim: Those families, where parents disagreed about warmth, were linked to more marital distress.
post: Mothers, fathers, and two school-age children from each family were interviewed at home. Parents reported whether they showed more warmth to one child or treated them equally. In some families one parent said equal and the other said unequal. Those families, where parents disagreed about warmth, were linked to more marital distress.

claim: People who said achievement mattered more to them were more likely to come to believe the false achievement event had happened.
post: People rated how sure they were that certain events happened in their childhood. Two weeks later they got a made-up "computer profile" saying a false achievement event and a false friendship event had happened to them, and they imagined and described both. People who said achievement mattered more to them were more likely to come to believe the false achievement event had happened.

claim: Ability and conscientiousness together explained almost as much of the differences in scores as all measures combined, and far more than family background.
post: Students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland took their big school exams at age 16. Researchers checked how well family background, mental ability, and conscientiousness (being careful and hardworking) lined up with exam scores. Ability and conscientiousness together explained almost as much of the differences in scores as all measures combined, and far more than family background.

claim: The pigeons mostly preferred the single unbroken wait over the split one.
post: Pigeons chose between two keys they could peck. Both keys led to a reward after the same total wait. On one key the wait was a single stretch, and on the other it was split into two stretches back to back. The pigeons mostly preferred the single unbroken wait over the split one.
journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior

claim: How good an example the item was had no effect on answer speed beyond what how easily the category came to mind already explained.
post: People saw a category name and the name of an item, and decided whether the item belonged to the category. For some, the category appeared 800 milliseconds before the item. For others, the item came first. How good an example the item was had no effect on answer speed beyond what how easily the category came to mind already explained.
journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition

claim: The Norwegian students' scores were more moderate than the American students' scores.
post: University students in Norway and in the United States filled out a questionnaire about how they were working out who they are. It covered beliefs and values as well as close relationships. The Norwegian students' scores were more moderate than the American students' scores.

claim: All 25 happened on days calmer than that month's average.
post: People reported sudden, intense paranormal experiences, like sensing that a friend or family member was sick or had died. For 25 published cases, researchers looked up how disturbed Earth's magnetic field was on each day. All 25 happened on days calmer than that month's average.

claim: The romantic-mindset men were willing to spend more on showy luxuries than the other men, but not more on necessities.
post: Some men were put in the mindset of wanting to attract a romantic partner, and others were not. Then the men said how much they would spend on luxuries and on basic necessities. The romantic-mindset men were willing to spend more on showy luxuries than the other men, but not more on necessities.
journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

claim: Among children of the same age and vocabulary score, those better at repeating numbers in reverse did better on both kinds of tasks.
post: Preschoolers repeated strings of numbers, some in the same order and some in reverse. They also did tasks about what another person wrongly believes, and similar tasks that used photographs instead of beliefs. Among children of the same age and vocabulary score, those better at repeating numbers in reverse did better on both kinds of tasks.

claim: People who saw the warm version rated his appearance, mannerisms, and accent as appealing, while people who saw the cold version rated them as irritating.
post: People watched a videotaped interview with a college instructor who spoke English with a European accent. It was the same man in both versions, but in one he acted warm and friendly and in the other cold and distant. People who saw the warm version rated his appearance, mannerisms, and accent as appealing, while people who saw the cold version rated them as irritating.
journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

claim: Body responses to the in-between clips differed from those to the funny and painful ones, in strength and in pattern.
post: Women watched 45 short video clips while sensors tracked their body responses. Some clips were funny, like a slip of the tongue during wedding vows. Some were painful accidents, and some were in between, like a boy falling off a treadmill. Body responses to the in-between clips differed from those to the funny and painful ones, in strength and in pattern.

claim: In schools with a more positive climate, victimization was less tied to feeling detached from others, but more tied to feeling less accomplished.
post: Teachers at middle and high schools across China filled out a survey about being victimized at work, how burned out they felt, and how positive their school's climate was. In schools with a more positive climate, victimization was less tied to feeling detached from others, but more tied to feeling less accomplished.

claim: Those people valued following rules and feeling secure more, and valued independence and excitement less, than people who were less focused on avoiding losses.
post: People answered questions about how they go after goals and what matters most to them in life. Some were mainly focused on avoiding mistakes and losses. Those people valued following rules and feeling secure more, and valued independence and excitement less, than people who were less focused on avoiding losses.

claim: People responded faster and more accurately to the more iconic words.
post: People decided as fast as they could whether strings of letters were real words. Some words were more iconic, meaning their sound resembles their meaning. People responded faster and more accurately to the more iconic words.

claim: Their coffee dropped from almost nine cups a day to under three, a 69% cut.
post: Three heavy coffee drinkers tracked and charted every cup they drank. Each got a daily limit that slowly got lower. They won money for staying under the limit and lost part of a deposit they had put down when they went over. Their coffee dropped from almost nine cups a day to under three, a 69% cut.

claim: Children who once had a language disorder were much worse at telling the two apart than children with typical language development.
post: Children and adults watched a flashing explosion-shaped figure while hearing a beep. They judged whether the flash and the beep happened at exactly the same time, when the beep came anywhere from no delay to half a second off. Children who once had a language disorder were much worse at telling the two apart than children with typical language development.
journal: Journal of Speech Language and Hearing Research

claim: Teens in the identity program explored their background more than the comparison group, and then felt more settled about what it means to them.
post: Teenagers were randomly assigned to one of two programs. One was a program built to get them thinking about their ethnic and racial background. The other was a comparison program that gave them attention but wasn't about identity. Teens in the identity program explored their background more than the comparison group, and then felt more settled about what it means to them.

claim: In both groups, higher rating-scale scores went with higher computer scores.
post: People with borderline personality disorder and people without it each did an interview, and their answers were scored two ways. A rating scale judged how well they understood their own and others' thoughts and feelings. A computer program scored the same answers by counting 54 word patterns. In both groups, higher rating-scale scores went with higher computer scores.

claim: When the issue mattered to them, students were swayed mostly by how strong the arguments were, and when it did not, they were swayed mostly by how expert the source seemed.
post: Undergraduates read a persuasive message that argued against what they already believed. Some read strong arguments and some weak ones, and the message came from a source that was either an expert or not. For some students the issue mattered a lot to them personally, and for others it hardly did. When the issue mattered to them, students were swayed mostly by how strong the arguments were, and when it did not, they were swayed mostly by how expert the source seemed.
journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

claim: Personality explained a substantial part of the differences in test scores and grades.
post: Two large sets of data held people's achievement test scores, their school grades, and measures of their personality. The researchers checked how much of the differences between people in scores and grades lined up with differences in personality. Personality explained a substantial part of the differences in test scores and grades.

claim: Students became more conscientious when assigned to conscientious peers, more open-minded when assigned to open-minded peers, and more competitive when assigned to competitive peers.
post: University students were randomly assigned to study groups. Students became more conscientious when assigned to conscientious peers, more open-minded when assigned to open-minded peers, and more competitive when assigned to competitive peers.
journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

claim: Stressed people's choices did not shift away from the food they were full of, compared with the warm-water group.
post: Some people held a hand in ice water for three minutes while a stranger watched; others used warm water, unwatched. Then everyone learned which screen symbols won chocolate milk or orange juice, and later ate one of those foods until full. Stressed people's choices did not shift away from the food they were full of, compared with the warm-water group.

claim: Students who attended the In Our Own Voice presentation improved more in knowledge and attitudes than the career talk group, on all three measures.
post: College students answered questions about what they knew and how they felt about mental illness. Then some attended a presentation from the In Our Own Voice program, and others attended a talk about careers in psychology. Everyone answered the same questions again. Students who attended the In Our Own Voice presentation improved more in knowledge and attitudes than the career talk group, on all three measures.

claim: The students taught that stress can help reported less math anxiety and did better on the exam than the students told to ignore it.
post: Community college students in a math course got a message before a class exam. Some were taught that a racing heart and other signs of stress can help them perform. Others were told to ignore their stress. The students taught that stress can help reported less math anxiety and did better on the exam than the students told to ignore it.

claim: Among light drinkers, that extra fading of bad feelings was larger for ordinary events than for alcohol events.
post: People were asked about events from their lives, some involving alcohol and some not, and about how much they drank in a typical week. Past unpleasant feelings usually fade faster than pleasant ones. Among light drinkers, that extra fading of bad feelings was larger for ordinary events than for alcohol events.

claim: After the video, all four supervisors mastered the skills.
post: Four clinic supervisors role-played giving feedback to a pretend therapist. At different times, each one then watched a video showing how to give good feedback, with a voice explaining each step. Their feedback was scored on eight skills before and after the video. After the video, all four supervisors mastered the skills.

claim: Marines who felt betrayed had more PTSD symptoms, and the link ran through anger.
post: Marines who had fought in Afghanistan answered questions one month after coming home. They reported times they were in danger, times they broke their own moral values, and times trusted others let them down. Eight months later they reported their anger and PTSD symptoms. Marines who felt betrayed had more PTSD symptoms, and the link ran through anger.
journal: Psychological Trauma: Theory, Research, Practice, and Policy

claim: Items from different classes were judged as farther apart than in the series with no classes.
post: People judged items in a series on a physical scale. For some, the items were split into classes that followed the scale, with smaller ones in one class and larger ones in another. For others, the series had no classes. Items from different classes were judged as farther apart than in the series with no classes.

claim: Musicians were not fooled by the mismatch on any syllable, while the others were fooled on several.
post: People watched videos of a face saying a syllable while hearing a different syllable, then wrote down what they heard. Half were trained conservatory musicians and half had no music training. Musicians were not fooled by the mismatch on any syllable, while the others were fooled on several.

claim: Symptoms dropped in every group, with no clear difference between the standard and modified versions.
post: Adults with social anxiety did a computer attention task for 15 minutes, twice a week, for four weeks. Some got a standard version and others a modified version meant to shift attention. Some did it in a lab and others at home. Symptoms dropped in every group, with no clear difference between the standard and modified versions.

claim: The Chinese bilinguals grouped objects more by how they relate to each other, and less by category, than European Americans did, in both languages.
post: Bilingual Chinese people and European Americans organized objects, and the Chinese bilinguals did it in either English or Chinese. The Chinese bilinguals grouped objects more by how they relate to each other, and less by category, than European Americans did, in both languages.
journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

claim: People who reported more binge episodes in the interview also reported more on the questionnaire.
post: People with binge eating disorder were asked about their eating habits in two ways: a face-to-face interview and a written questionnaire. Both asked how many times they had binged. People who reported more binge episodes in the interview also reported more on the questionnaire.
journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology

claim: Rounds that ended in a near-miss were rated less pleasant than clear misses, but people said they wanted to keep playing more.
post: People played a slot machine game where they won money only if two icons matched. On some rounds they picked their own icon, and on others the computer picked it. Rounds that ended in a near-miss were rated less pleasant than clear misses, but people said they wanted to keep playing more.

claim: Lying responses were slower than truthful ones, and brain recordings also showed more mental effort for lying.
post: People saw statements about attitudes, some they strongly agreed with and some they strongly disagreed with. For some statements they pressed the button for their true answer. For others they were told to press the opposite button, as a lie. Lying responses were slower than truthful ones, and brain recordings also showed more mental effort for lying.

claim: They found that a shift over time in this willingness can look like people getting worse at telling real events from background noise.
post: People kept watch for rare but important events over a long stretch of time. The researchers tracked how willing people were to say they had spotted one. They found that a shift over time in this willingness can look like people getting worse at telling real events from background noise.

claim: Problematic traits were partly predicted by the other two measures combined.
post: People in China who had offended were assessed four times over one year. The assessments covered how well they handle their sense of self and relationships, their everyday personality traits, and their problematic traits. Problematic traits were partly predicted by the other two measures combined.

claim: The events in their memories and their feelings while recalling them predicted how distressed they said they were.
post: College students each shared 10 memories that helped define who they were. Each memory was scored for the kinds of events in it and the emotion people felt when recalling it. The students also filled out a questionnaire that measured how distressed they felt. The events in their memories and their feelings while recalling them predicted how distressed they said they were.

claim: Both anxious groups spent longer looking at the disgusted faces than the not-anxious students did.
post: People looked at grids of faces, eight disgusted and eight neutral, for six seconds each while their eye movements were tracked. Some had social anxiety disorder, some were very socially anxious students, and some were students who were not anxious. Both anxious groups spent longer looking at the disgusted faces than the not-anxious students did.

claim: Women who watched their looks more and felt more body shame reported less sexual satisfaction.
post: College women in the UK filled out questionnaires. They covered media beauty ideals, how often they watched how their body looked, how ashamed they felt of it, and how satisfied they were with sex. Women who watched their looks more and felt more body shame reported less sexual satisfaction.

claim: Children judged the individuals who ate the other group's berries negatively, less so as they got older.
post: Children and adults learned about two made-up groups, Hibbles and Glerks, that typically ate different kinds of berries. They then judged individuals who ate the berries typical of their own group or of the other group. Children judged the individuals who ate the other group's berries negatively, less so as they got older.

claim: People nudged to feel romantic nostalgia reported stronger benefits for their relationship than the others.
post: People in romantic relationships were nudged to feel nostalgic about times with their partner. In one experiment they did a writing task, and in another they listened to music. Others were not given that nudge. People nudged to feel romantic nostalgia reported stronger benefits for their relationship than the others.
journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships

claim: But that link disappeared once their depression, anxiety and hostility were taken into account, and depression explained most of it.
post: Patients being treated for pain filled out questionnaires about their moods, their pain, and traits of borderline personality disorder. People with more of those traits reported more pain. But that link disappeared once their depression, anxiety and hostility were taken into account, and depression explained most of it.

claim: Sounds that adults rated as easier to say were the ones three-year-olds had mastered better.
post: Adults rated how physically easy it is to say different consonant sounds at the start of a word. Those ratings were then compared with earlier data on how well three-year-olds had mastered the same sounds. Sounds that adults rated as easier to say were the ones three-year-olds had mastered better.
journal: Journal of Speech and Hearing Research

claim: Bubbles were smaller in the markets where only some traders knew more than the others.
post: People traded in experimental markets where they could know about upcoming dividends. In some markets everyone knew, in some no one knew, and in some only some traders knew. Bubbles were smaller in the markets where only some traders knew more than the others.

claim: Knowing safety aids were available hurt fear reduction about as much as using them, compared with having none.
post: People with a strong fear of enclosed spaces went through treatment that meant facing those spaces. Some had safety aids available, some actually used them, and some had none. Others got a placebo treatment or waited. Knowing safety aids were available hurt fear reduction about as much as using them, compared with having none.
journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology

claim: They preferred colors that followed 20 pecks over matching colors that followed one peck.
post: Pigeons pecked a key either once or 20 times, then saw a pair of colors, one that led to food and one that did not. Each effort level had its own colors. Later they chose between colors from the two levels. They preferred colors that followed 20 pecks over matching colors that followed one peck.

claim: Every child more than doubled their rate of correctly read words compared with before.
post: Third and fourth graders practiced reading words from drill sheets that looked like a car racetrack, with timing and a correction whenever they missed a word. Each child's reading was measured before the sheets started and again during. Every child more than doubled their rate of correctly read words compared with before.

claim: Children showed more than four times as many of these skills as they did before the teaching.
post: Teachers in one preschool class taught all 16 children skills like following instructions, waiting, and making friends. They taught during normal activities like circle time and meals, using role play, modeling, and feedback. Children showed more than four times as many of these skills as they did before the teaching.

claim: Compared with the other gamblers, those with problems had a stronger tendency to pull gambling pictures than neutral ones.
post: Gamblers with moderate to high gambling problems and gamblers without problems did an online task, pressing keys to pull pictures toward them or push them away. Some pictures were about gambling, matched to each person's usual games. Others were neutral. Compared with the other gamblers, those with problems had a stronger tendency to pull gambling pictures than neutral ones.

claim: Once the other three parts were taken into account, only the interpersonal part was linked to cocaine dependence.
post: Men in a Chicago-area jail were interviewed about their lives, and the answers were used to score four parts of psychopathy. Another interview covered their use of alcohol, cannabis, cocaine and opioids. Once the other three parts were taken into account, only the interpersonal part was linked to cocaine dependence.

claim: Spoken naming also improved after the therapy, because the written word could give the same kind of sound hint.
post: A patient with a reading disorder was taught which sound goes with each letter. The patient still could not blend separate sounds into a whole word, but could say a word's first sound, and that worked as a hint for reading it. Spoken naming also improved after the therapy, because the written word could give the same kind of sound hint.

claim: Students who blamed bad events on causes that last and that affect everything in life were more depressed a month later.
post: College students filled out a questionnaire about why bad things happen to them, plus a depression questionnaire. A month later they filled out both again. Students who blamed bad events on causes that last and that affect everything in life were more depressed a month later.

claim: People found the explanations with the name more satisfying.
post: People read explanations for why a person behaved a certain way. Some explanations appealed to a named tendency or condition, and others gave the same explanation without the name. People found the explanations with the name more satisfying.

claim: Those with agoraphobia recalled more of the pieces of information from the fear-related passages than the others did.
post: People with agoraphobia, a strong fear of leaving safe places, and people without it tried to recall five passages. Three contained information related to that fear and two were neutral. Those with agoraphobia recalled more of the pieces of information from the fear-related passages than the others did.

claim: Patients who scored higher on resilience had lower emotional distress, even after accounting for other differences between patients.
post: Hospital patients being treated for cancer filled out two questionnaires. One measured how well they cope with hardship, called resilience. The other measured anxiety and depression. Patients who scored higher on resilience had lower emotional distress, even after accounting for other differences between patients.

claim: Clinicians with less traditional beliefs rated the patient more favorably when he was labeled black than when he was labeled white.
post: Black clinicians read the same made-up case about a man with sexual problems. Some were told he was black and others were told he was white. They also filled out a questionnaire about traditional social beliefs. Clinicians with less traditional beliefs rated the patient more favorably when he was labeled black than when he was labeled white.

claim: Both how likely and how long each predicted people's usual anxiety scores, and each added something the other did not.
post: People went through the items on a common anxiety questionnaire, such as feeling tense or worried. For each item they answered three questions: how much of the time they felt it, how likely they were to feel it when stressed, and how long it lasted once it started. Both how likely and how long each predicted people's usual anxiety scores, and each added something the other did not.

claim: Those who read evidence that went against their belief rated educational research as less able to answer this question, and trusted its sources less, than those who read evidence that agreed.
post: Future teachers said what they believed about making struggling students repeat a school year. Then they read scientific evidence that either backed up their belief or went against it. Those who read evidence that went against their belief rated educational research as less able to answer this question, and trusted its sources less, than those who read evidence that agreed.

claim: High-anxiety people felt and acted more anxious and thought they were more aroused, but their actual physiological activation did not differ.
post: People who were high or low in social anxiety gave an impromptu speech. Researchers measured how anxious they felt and acted, how aroused they thought their bodies were, and how aroused their bodies actually were. High-anxiety people felt and acted more anxious and thought they were more aroused, but their actual physiological activation did not differ.

claim: Older typists with high skill did worse only at choosing the right key.
post: Typists of different ages and skill levels did simple tasks, like hitting one key when a letter appeared or two keys in a row. Older typists with low skill did worse than younger ones at both choosing the right key and moving the finger. Older typists with high skill did worse only at choosing the right key.

claim: Learning one kind of task helped with the other kind, except when the first memory had been made stable.
post: People learned a movement skill and then a list of words, or the words first and then the skill. For some, the first memory was made stable, so nothing could disrupt it. Learning one kind of task helped with the other kind, except when the first memory had been made stable.

claim: Often, the children treated an "or" sentence as if it said "and," so both things had to be true.
post: Preschool children heard sentences with the word "or," some of them also containing "every." The researchers checked how the children understood each sentence. Often, the children treated an "or" sentence as if it said "and," so both things had to be true.

claim: Teens who grew up better off were greedier, and this held for only children but not for teens with siblings.
post: Teenagers in China filled out questionnaires about how well off their family was growing up and how greedy they tend to be. Some were only children and others had siblings. Teens who grew up better off were greedier, and this held for only children but not for teens with siblings.

claim: Only infants who had napped remembered the actions.
post: Infants aged 6 and 12 months saw novel actions demonstrated. Some then took a nap of at least 30 minutes and others did not. Later they were tested on whether they remembered the actions. Only infants who had napped remembered the actions.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

claim: When the outer ovals pulled answers toward their tilt, answers were more precise, with less error overall, than with no outer ovals.
post: People stared at a dot while a tilted oval flashed off to the side, between two other ovals. They turned a bar to match the middle oval's tilt, while the outer ovals' tilt changed from trial to trial. When the outer ovals pulled answers toward their tilt, answers were more precise, with less error overall, than with no outer ovals.

claim: Both 3-year-olds and 4-year-olds passed the tasks without direct questions, but only the 4-year-olds passed the ones with them.
post: Young children did two kinds of tasks about a person who believes something that isn't true. In some tasks the children were asked outright about that belief, and in others they weren't. Both 3-year-olds and 4-year-olds passed the tasks without direct questions, but only the 4-year-olds passed the ones with them.

claim: Within the same person, thoughts they tried to escape or avoid were judged more disapprovingly than thoughts they tried to think through.
post: Students filled out a questionnaire about seven unpleasant thoughts that had popped into their heads uninvited. For each one, they said how they dealt with it and how they judged it. Within the same person, thoughts they tried to escape or avoid were judged more disapprovingly than thoughts they tried to think through.

claim: People reminded of how common atheists are distrusted them less.
post: Some people were given reminders that atheists are common, and others were not. Then they rated how much they distrust atheists. People reminded of how common atheists are distrusted them less.

claim: The two groups described their families in much the same way, but how teens described their family was strongly linked to how they saw themselves.
post: Teenagers from a clinic and matched teenagers not from a clinic filled out two questionnaires. One asked about closeness, parenting style and conflict in their family. The other asked how they saw themselves. The two groups described their families in much the same way, but how teens described their family was strongly linked to how they saw themselves.

claim: Working-class Americans were more influenced by others' choices than middle-class Americans.
post: Working-class and middle-class Americans decided which products to buy after learning what other people had chosen. Working-class Americans were more influenced by others' choices than middle-class Americans.

claim: Children picked the right event for 'the girl is fezzing' but not for 'the tall girl is fezzing'.
post: Preschoolers heard a made-up verb in a sentence while watching events, such as 'the girl is fezzing' or 'the tall girl is fezzing'. Then they pointed to the event they thought the verb meant. Children picked the right event for 'the girl is fezzing' but not for 'the tall girl is fezzing'.

claim: Students who had completed college English were more likely to pass than students still at the catch-up level.
post: Students at a large city community college took a psychology course with a lot of reading and writing. School records showed the highest English class each had finished: regular college English, or a catch-up class for weaker skills. Students who had completed college English were more likely to pass than students still at the catch-up level.

claim: Those who spotted it better also scored higher on a general anxiety questionnaire.
post: People saw a face flash for a split second, then get covered by a neutral face. After each, they said whether the flashed face looked fearful. Some people could reliably spot the fear and others could not. Those who spotted it better also scored higher on a general anxiety questionnaire.

claim: They preferred adjectives closest to the noun, then numbers, then this/that, most strongly for adjectives versus this/that.
post: English speakers learned a made-up language from cartoon pictures, like a red ball. Each person learned two kinds of describing words, then picked between two word orders for a phrase they were never taught, like "two red balls." They preferred adjectives closest to the noun, then numbers, then this/that, most strongly for adjectives versus this/that.
journal: Glossa: a journal of general linguistics

claim: Students in the program raised their grade point average from 1.73 to 2.39, while the others' grades did not change much.
post: Community college students who felt very anxious about tests joined a nine-session program. They learned to relax their muscles, then worked through a list of 25 test-related situations that made them nervous. Other anxious students got no program. Students in the program raised their grade point average from 1.73 to 2.39, while the others' grades did not change much.

claim: Women with L were less likely than women with H to be weak free-riders, who give little to the pot.
post: Women and men chose how much money to put into a shared group pot. Each player had one of two versions of the MAOA gene, called L or H. Women with L were less likely than women with H to be weak free-riders, who give little to the pot.
journal: Journal of Neuroscience Psychology and Economics

claim: After the extra practice, the boys named and asked for things more often than before.
post: Preschool boys with autism or a similar diagnosis did 100 extra rounds of naming practice each day. Researchers counted how often each boy named something or asked for something on his own, during short checks at free play, lunch, and in the hallway. After the extra practice, the boys named and asked for things more often than before.
journal: Journal of Early and Intensive Behavior Intervention

claim: Women who used diet pills or laxatives were more likely to be diagnosed within the next 1 to 3 years than women who did not.
post: Young women in the US were followed for years and asked every so often whether they took diet pills or laxatives to control their weight. Researchers then checked who later got a first eating disorder diagnosis. Women who used diet pills or laxatives were more likely to be diagnosed within the next 1 to 3 years than women who did not.

claim: People who read the "keeps 10%" version rated their chances of winning lower.
post: People from a gambling support forum read a message about a gambling game and rated their chances of winning on a 7-point scale. Half read "This game has an average percentage payout of 90%." The other half read "This game keeps 10% of all money bet on average." People who read the "keeps 10%" version rated their chances of winning lower.

claim: Greek toddlers seemed to get off to a slower start in learning early words than US toddlers.
post: Toddlers from Greek-speaking families, from about a year and a half to almost three, had their vocabulary checked with a Greek version of a US word survey. Their results were compared with those of US toddlers on the original survey. Greek toddlers seemed to get off to a slower start in learning early words than US toddlers.

claim: Being outgoing predicted job performance for managers and salespeople, jobs with a lot of dealing with people.
post: Workers in five kinds of jobs, such as police, managers and salespeople, had their personality measured and their job performance checked. The results of many earlier studies were pooled together. Being outgoing predicted job performance for managers and salespeople, jobs with a lot of dealing with people.

claim: Worked examples were especially helpful for people who were worse at switching, compared with solving problems alone.
post: Students solved three statistics problems on a computer, using textbook slides. Half also saw a worked-out solution for each problem, and half had only the textbook. All had earlier done a task measuring how easily they switch between mental tasks. Worked examples were especially helpful for people who were worse at switching, compared with solving problems alone.

claim: The PIL gave six themes and the SONG added four more, about how strongly people want to find meaning, so the SONG complemented the PIL.
post: Intro psychology students filled out two questionnaires about meaning and purpose in life, one called the PIL and one called the SONG. Researchers then checked how the answers grouped into themes. The PIL gave six themes and the SONG added four more, about how strongly people want to find meaning, so the SONG complemented the PIL.

claim: Most of these children flipped mainly letters that face right, like B, D and E, the opposite of the usual pattern.
post: Young children wrote their own names, going from right to left instead of the usual left to right. Children who write left to right tend to flip letters that face left, like J. Most of these children flipped mainly letters that face right, like B, D and E, the opposite of the usual pattern.

claim: Liking company and acting on impulse showed up as two separate traits, only partly related, in both groups.
post: People filled out a 70-question personality questionnaire about being outgoing, being anxious, and whether they were being honest about themselves. Researchers checked which answers tended to go together, then repeated this in a second, similar group of the same size. Liking company and acting on impulse showed up as two separate traits, only partly related, in both groups.
journal: British Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology

claim: Students who slept more hours reported fewer of these problems and behaviors than students who slept less.
post: High school students wrote down their usual school-night bedtime and wake-up time. They also said how often in the past two weeks they felt sad, hopeless or tense, and whether they used things like alcohol, tobacco or drugs. Students who slept more hours reported fewer of these problems and behaviors than students who slept less.

claim: A flipped layout made a reliable difference for the right half, but not for the left.
post: People judged whether two stacked words were related. Sometimes the layout matched real life, like ATTIC above BASEMENT, and sometimes it was flipped. The words were flashed to only the left or only the right half of the brain. A flipped layout made a reliable difference for the right half, but not for the left.

claim: People who saw one charity gave more to the low-administration one, but people who saw both gave more to the one that saved more lives.
post: People imagined giving money to a made-up charity. Some saw just one charity, while others saw two side by side. One charity spent little on administration, and the other saved more than twice as many lives per dollar. People who saw one charity gave more to the low-administration one, but people who saw both gave more to the one that saved more lives.

claim: Some learned right away, some only after being told the rule, and some kept clicking it even after being told.
post: People clicked on two planets on a screen to earn points. Later, clicking one planet sometimes brought up a spaceship, followed by an attack that took away some of their points. Most people learned to avoid that planet, but not everyone. Some learned right away, some only after being told the rule, and some kept clicking it even after being told.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

claim: Beliefs about the virus fully explained why dark traits went with fewer precautions, and partly explained why they went with more hoarding.
post: People in Poland answered questions about their personality, their beliefs about the coronavirus, and what they did during the pandemic. People with more "dark" traits, like being manipulative or callous, took fewer precautions and hoarded more. Beliefs about the virus fully explained why dark traits went with fewer precautions, and partly explained why they went with more hoarding.

claim: The vast majority of both children and adults felt negative about fractions, even though they felt positive about whole numbers.
post: Children and adults were asked how they felt about math, once when thinking about whole numbers and once when thinking about fractions. Their math skill levels were also taken into account. The vast majority of both children and adults felt negative about fractions, even though they felt positive about whole numbers.

claim: People who expected to teach putted better than people who expected a test.
post: People studied golf-putting instructions and practiced putting. Some expected to teach another person how to putt afterward, and others expected to be tested on their own putting. A day later, everyone was tested on their putting. People who expected to teach putted better than people who expected a test.
journal: Journal of Motor Learning and Development

claim: Nearly a third of the speakers had no published papers on the topic they presented.
post: Researchers collected the lineups of keynote and invited speakers at state behavior analyst conferences over three years. For each talk, they searched Google Scholar for the speaker's published research papers on that talk's topic. Nearly a third of the speakers had no published papers on the topic they presented.

claim: The coached parents were better at setting limits in a positive way than the parents who got no coaching.
post: Parents of preschool twins took part in a 'don't touch' task, where they had to get each child to stay away from attractive toys. Some parents then got five sessions of coaching with video feedback on how they interacted with their kids, and others got none. The coached parents were better at setting limits in a positive way than the parents who got no coaching.

claim: The borderline group scored higher on six of the test's 13 standard scales.
post: Male veterans staying in a hospital took a standard personality test called the MMPI. Some had been diagnosed with borderline personality disorder, and others with different personality disorders. The borderline group scored higher on six of the test's 13 standard scales.

claim: The more people said they rethink situations, the less in sync parts of the amygdala, an emotion area, were with two other brain areas.
post: Healthy adults filled out a questionnaire about how often they handle feelings by rethinking the situation. They also had their brains scanned while resting, to see which areas rose and fell in activity together. The more people said they rethink situations, the less in sync parts of the amygdala, an emotion area, were with two other brain areas.

claim: Students who were kind to themselves, saw their struggles as part of being human, and were mindful lived healthier lives.
post: Undergraduates filled in two questionnaires: one on how they treat themselves when things go wrong, and one on their health habits. Researchers looked at which parts of self-compassion went with a healthier lifestyle. Students who were kind to themselves, saw their struggles as part of being human, and were mindful lived healthier lives.

claim: Surrender at the start best explained mystical experiences, and preoccupation best explained challenging, dread-filled ones.
post: People who had taken psilocybin on their own in the past year filled out an online survey. They looked back on their state of mind at the start and on what the experience was like. Surrender at the start best explained mystical experiences, and preoccupation best explained challenging, dread-filled ones.
journal: Psychology of Consciousness: Theory, Research, and Practice

claim: Many people sang at least one song at the right pitch.
post: People sang two popular songs from memory, and their pitch was compared with the pitch of the original recordings. Many people sang at least one song at the right pitch.

claim: Early on, people read faster after a sensible first word than after a nonsensical one, but later, a sensible unrelated word gave no benefit.
post: People read sentences while a tracker followed their eyes. One word was swapped for another just as their eyes reached it, and the first word either made sense in the sentence or didn't. Early on, people read faster after a sensible first word than after a nonsensical one, but later, a sensible unrelated word gave no benefit.
journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition

claim: For all four humor styles, differences between people were explained by genes and by experiences that twins don't share, not by the home they grew up in together.
post: Adult twins in the UK, some identical and some fraternal, filled out a questionnaire at home about their sense of humor. It asked how much they agreed with statements like "I laugh and joke a lot with my friends." For all four humor styles, differences between people were explained by genes and by experiences that twins don't share, not by the home they grew up in together.

claim: Students read more words correctly when they had repeated the word out loud, including later tests and words read in sentences.
post: Students with developmental disabilities learned to read new words one-on-one with a teacher. When a student made a mistake on some words, the teacher said the word and the student repeated it. On other words, the teacher said the word while the student just looked at the card. Students read more words correctly when they had repeated the word out loud, including later tests and words read in sentences.

claim: The students paid more attention to their work and did better on it when they had a choice than when they did not.
post: Five students with or at risk for emotional disturbance did their schoolwork in a regular classroom. Some of the time they were given a choice about which assignment to do, and other times they were not. The students paid more attention to their work and did better on it when they had a choice than when they did not.
journal: Preventing School Failure: Alternative Education for Children and Youth

claim: For soldiers with high fear, more head injuries went with more stress symptoms; for those with low fear, the link was weaker.
post: Soldiers who had been through trauma answered questions on a laptop. They reported how many likely head injuries they'd had, how much they fear that trouble focusing means going crazy, and their stress symptoms. For soldiers with high fear, more head injuries went with more stress symptoms; for those with low fear, the link was weaker.

claim: Afterward, both the people who did the task and the watchers still judged the performers' abilities in line with the fake feedback.
post: People tried a new kind of task and were told, falsely, that they had done well or badly. Other people watched and listened in. Then everyone was told the scores were made up and random. Afterward, both the people who did the task and the watchers still judged the performers' abilities in line with the fake feedback.
journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

claim: More thought-and-behavior techniques without them did not.
post: Clients at a counseling center rated their most recent therapy session. They said how strong their bond with the therapist felt, and how much the therapist used feelings-and-relationships techniques and thought-and-behavior techniques. When the bond was strong, more feelings-and-relationships techniques went with better change after the session. More thought-and-behavior techniques without them did not.

claim: Among the women who finished the therapy, PTSD went away in 87% of them, and their depression and guilt dropped a lot.
post: Women who had been abused by a partner and had PTSD were randomly put into two groups. Some started a course of trauma therapy right away, and others were put on a waiting list to start later. Among the women who finished the therapy, PTSD went away in 87% of them, and their depression and guilt dropped a lot.
journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology

claim: Family scores were more strongly linked to teens' self-ratings for those without a close friend than for those with one.
post: Parents filled out a questionnaire about how close and flexible their family was. Their young teens named their friends, rated their best friendship, and rated how well they were doing. Family scores were more strongly linked to teens' self-ratings for those without a close friend than for those with one.

claim: Twitches were smaller when the sentence was about an action with that same body part than when it was abstract.
post: People listened to sentences about hand actions, foot actions, or abstract ideas. Meanwhile a magnetic pulse over the brain made their hand or foot muscles twitch. Twitches were smaller when the sentence was about an action with that same body part than when it was abstract.

claim: People with panic disorder remembered the threatening words better than the positive and neutral ones, and the other group did not.
post: People with panic disorder and people without it did two word memory tasks. One was a fast recognition task, the other was recalling words freely. The words were threatening, positive, or neutral. People with panic disorder remembered the threatening words better than the positive and neutral ones, and the other group did not.

claim: The new group's outcomes were nearly identical to the original group's.
post: At-risk kindergartners went through an early program called First Step to Success. This was a repeat run with a new group of children, and the results were compared with those from the original test of the program. The new group's outcomes were nearly identical to the original group's.
journal: Journal of Emotional and Behavioral Disorders

claim: Women preferred the altruistic men, especially for long-term relationships.
post: Women saw photographs of men who were more or less attractive, each with a description of how he behaved in different situations, altruistically or not. They rated how desirable each man was. Women preferred the altruistic men, especially for long-term relationships.

claim: The imagery practice helped the children's motor skills about as much as the traditional training did.
post: Children who had trouble with movement and coordination were randomly split into three groups. One group practiced imagining movements with an interactive CD-ROM, one did traditional movement training, and one was put on a waiting list. The imagery practice helped the children's motor skills about as much as the traditional training did.

claim: The OCD group and the relatives were both slower than the third group at choosing where to look.
post: People did eye-movement tasks. Some had OCD, some were healthy close relatives of people with OCD, and some had no family history of it. In some tasks they chose for themselves where to look; in another, what they saw guided their eyes. The OCD group and the relatives were both slower than the third group at choosing where to look.
journal: European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience

claim: On the end-of-week tests, every student learned more new words when they had corrected after each word.
post: Five elementary school students with learning disabilities practiced spelling by listening to a tape that read out a word list, then writing each word. For half the words, they checked and fixed their spelling after each word. For the other half, they waited until they had tried all 10 words. On the end-of-week tests, every student learned more new words when they had corrected after each word.

claim: The threatening words sped up responses to alcohol words only for alcohol-dependent people who had been emotionally abused as children.
post: People with alcohol dependence and people without it did a word task on a screen. A threatening word, like one about being hurt or put down, came first, and then a word about alcohol or a neutral word. The threatening words sped up responses to alcohol words only for alcohol-dependent people who had been emotionally abused as children.

claim: A year later, more people in the therapist-guided group had stopped binge eating: 64% versus 45%.
post: Adults who often binge ate were randomly split into two groups. One group got eight short sessions over 12 weeks with a therapist who walked them through a self-help program. The other group got the usual care their health plan offered. A year later, more people in the therapist-guided group had stopped binge eating: 64% versus 45%.
journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology

claim: People did better on the timing task and worse on the space task when it was near their hands than when it was far.
post: People did two vision tasks: noticing a short gap in time, and noticing a small gap in space. Sometimes what they looked at was near their hands, and sometimes it was far from their hands. People did better on the timing task and worse on the space task when it was near their hands than when it was far.

claim: Those who had lost control first showed a smaller brain response to being left out, and said they felt less excluded, than the others.
post: People played an on-screen ball-tossing game with two other players, with brain activity recorded. Some first played a version in which they lost control. Then everyone started getting the ball less often. Those who had lost control first showed a smaller brain response to being left out, and said they felt less excluded, than the others.

claim: Their rate of specific praise went up compared with before the feedback, and it was still higher 3 months after the emails ended.
post: Elementary school teachers got regular emails with visual feedback on how often they used specific praise, which means praise that names what a student did well. Their rate of specific praise went up compared with before the feedback, and it was still higher 3 months after the emails ended.

claim: People walked faster when music depended on speeding up, and slower when it depended on slowing down.
post: People walked on a treadmill without a motor, at whatever pace they liked, while music played. In some parts of the session the music played no matter how fast they walked. In others it played only while they sped up, or only while they slowed down. People walked faster when music depended on speeding up, and slower when it depended on slowing down.
journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior

claim: Students with higher achievement rated themselves higher, but countries with higher average achievement had lower average self-ratings.
post: Students in many countries rated how good they felt they were at math and science, and those ratings were compared with their achievement. This was checked two ways: student by student, and country by country using averages. Students with higher achievement rated themselves higher, but countries with higher average achievement had lower average self-ratings.

claim: Faces that looked more masculine were picked as better war leaders, and faces that looked more feminine were picked as better peace leaders.
post: People looked at black-and-white photos of faces with hair and ears cropped out. They rated how much each person looked like a leader during a war, or during a time of peace, and how masculine or feminine each face looked. Faces that looked more masculine were picked as better war leaders, and faces that looked more feminine were picked as better peace leaders.

claim: The students lied most on the phone and least in email.
post: College students kept a diary for a week. They wrote down their social conversations and every time they lied in them, whether face to face, on the phone, by instant message, or by email. The students lied most on the phone and least in email.
journal: Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems

claim: Ten of 11 predicted scores were related to the other test's scores by more than chance.
